issues.body:
Hero run started on August 19th. This should be a terse log of status events and interventions since then.

```
./experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/trigger_hero.sh
```

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
August 20th: noticed that we are OOMing every ~3 hours.

We attempted interventions to adjust XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.83 (giving XLA more memory). This made things worse. 

--xla_gpu_memory_limit_slop_factor seems to be another promising tunable. Adjusting to 0.88 from the default 0.95 didn't help. Testing with 0.85 now.

In theory fraction 0.83 with slop 88 strictly dominates the baseline, as a followup to test if the lowered thresholds don't hold.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
We observed periodic host OOMs after several checkpoints. https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/200 . Restarting with the following changes:

1. Tensorstore restore parallelism bounded by a fixed budget
2. Checkpoint offload cache to 16GB
3. malloc_trim() calls after each checkpoint

in theory 2 will make checkpoints faster (fully async), and 3 will prevent the host OOM recurrence

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
`malloc_trim` was still inconsistently resulting in OOMs during checkpointing. Restarting on main with the jemalloc changes in.

Restores were hitting single worker stalls. Merged and running with #8584 . First restore after this change was successful, though it might have been luck/caching.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Memory sampling on the current `coord-memfix` instance isolates checkpoint-correlated retained RSS to writer tasks 0–127. Their median floor rose 11.7 GiB after the first save and 4.4 GiB after the second; tasks 128–175 stayed on the baseline slope. Each writer rank was assigned about 9.5–10.2 GiB, and `/proc` attributes the retained difference to anonymous memory across the four child Python processes.

The run contains #8609. The signature matches its documented persistent CUDA pinned-host BFC pool cost. The smaller second increment does not support projecting a fixed 30 GiB leak per save.

Incident record: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/227

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body: 🤖 Correction after tracing the current checkpoint path: the long-lived `GlobalAsyncCheckpointManager` keeps the completed TensorStore commit futures in `_commit_futures`; `wait_until_finished()` joins but does not clear them, and the writes allow indefinite source-buffer references. This mechanism predates #8609 and plausibly retains one staged checkpoint share per writer rank. PR #8599 contained a reviewed post-join cleanup for these futures, but that part did not land with #8609. The pinned-host BFC pool in #8609 remains an additional allocator-level floor that clearing the manager cannot purge. Updated evidence and safe cleanup boundaries: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/227

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body: 🤖 The loader-cache ablation is complete. On two trays with the Harrier mixture, global batch 1024, and sequence length 4096, the profiler-free 1 GB/process arm delivered 0.937 batches/s including cold start versus 0.956 batches/s at 125 GB/process. The hero runs at 19.9 s/step (0.050 batches/s), so the 1 GB cap has 18.6x headroom and bounds the decoded cache near 0.923 GiB/process. Report: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/235

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Paused for the #8870 debugging window and redeployed from main. A checkpoint was forced through the training-control endpoint before the cancel, so the pause cost about one step instead of the ~131 (~44 min, ~515 GPU-hours) that killing at a random point in the hourly temporary-checkpoint cycle would have discarded: `step-58014` committed 23:13:13Z and was verified complete (`manifest.json`, `manifest.ocdbt`, `metadata.json`, 28,098 objects, 5.36 TB). `/marin/hero-12d8b6f0-dee637-coord-e3052688` was cancelled at 23:14:12Z having last logged step 58.0k at loss 1.22.

The window ran 11 racks from 23:16Z to 00:40Z across two jobs and did not reproduce the hang: 164 steps then 71, 235 in total, at the hero's exact shape restored from the same `step-54000` the two failed attempts used. Details in #8870.

Redeployed at 00:41:36Z from a pristine worktree at `origin/main` `023ed7a24d` as `/marin/hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k-coord-95c15d9b`, run id `hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k`, submitted with `IRIS_USER=marin`. It carries two changes relative to the paused run: the pooled-wave fallback (#8884, which the paused run was already effectively running) and gate/router weight decay on by default at 0.02 annealed linearly to zero (#8833). The launch args were diffed against the paused run's own recorded argv and match on every field except run id, job name, `--initialize-from-checkpoint`, and the `--system-reason` string.

Resume verified: the gang placed in ~80 s, 177 tasks, and the restore names `step-58014` under the temporary root rather than falling back to the `step-54000` permanent, which would have discarded ~4,000 steps. First step 00:50:12Z; now training at ~18.4 s/step, MFU ~21%, loss ~1.24, continuous with the 1.22-1.25 before the pause, and logging to W&B as `hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k`.

Net cost: ~96 min of the 11 racks, of which ~84 was the window and ~9 startup.

Note for #8833: that experiment's launcher originally handed off from `step-54000`; #8890 repointed it at `step-58014` so the relaunch would not discard the day of training since. Its control is therefore the paused hero's own trajectory from 58014, not the step-54000 one.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Plan for today's redeployment of the hero on the ragged all-to-all transport, 2026-09-09. The live run `hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k` (commit `0908920c86`) is at step ~81.5k at 19.8 s/step, loss ~1.23.

Sequence: merge #8959 (QuACK 0.6.4, the grouped-GEMM scheduler fix) and #9043 (ragged transport and fp32 weights on device back as the hero default, reverting #8884), then force a checkpoint on the live run through the training-control endpoint about 70 minutes before the cutover, mark its metadata non-temporary so the hourly temporary save does not prune it, open the launcher PR pointing `trigger_hero.sh` at it under run id `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step<N>k`, let the old run train 200 steps past it as the paired control, cancel the old coordinator, and launch main from a pristine worktree as `IRIS_USER=marin`. Waiting for the next permanent checkpoint was rejected: step-84000 lands at ~07:00Z tomorrow and step-90000 on Thursday, and a forced checkpoint costs one step (the step-58014 precedent).

The new run carries, relative to the live one: the ragged transport with fp32 weights on device (#9043), one train-step executable per rank (#8911), the balanced ragged device kernel wheel (#8976), QuACK 0.6.4 (#8959), and the cross-entropy tile and FA4 padding fixes (#8960, #8961). The root cause of #8870 is still open; the strongest lead is a fabric fault on the racks that land at replica indices 8-10, which the trial cannot avoid.

Gate over the 200-step window against the old run on the same batches: loss within bf16 noise of the control after the ~0.006 nat dropless offset, drop fraction below 1e-3, MFU at or above the control's ~21%, no hang, retry, or watchdog. Anything short of that rolls back at once by relaunching `trigger_hero.sh` at `0908920c86`, which resumes the old run's own newest checkpoint. Runbook scripts (preflight with an NVLink counter sweep, cancel, launch, monitor, rollback) are being dry-run read-only against the cluster. A W&B report with both run sets over the trial window will be linked here before launch, along with each transition: forced checkpoint, cancel, launch, first steps, go/no-go.

issues.title: Hero Run / Ongoing Status

issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

comments.body:
🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Comparing our scaling law to prior runs. The main differences here is that the May recipe is at compute optimal, this run is at ~12x overtrained, and the 67B-A2B scaling law was at 100x overtrained. The 67B-A2B ran at 8k seqlen, and was therefore given a lower asympotote of 1.4 instead of 1.5. The May fit also inaccurately has an asympotote at 1.6 instead of 1.5. Main architecture change is we dropped from 4/256 level of sparsity to 4/192 level of sparsity (25% fewer total parameters, to fit on GB200 at this scale. Several other small features added. Overall, the scaling law looks reasonable and nothing looks off in the training dynamics or data. Grad norms look stable over the run, peaking at 25% into the run. These runs ran at oversized batch sizes, which may be slightly suppressing the gradient. Expecting the grad norm to climb higher on the hero run, but still peak at the same ~25% into the run. This will be good metric to monitor for issues. Drop rate jumps to 10 pct at very start, then drops to 0, then climbs to ~4pct over the run. Slightly increasing as we scale. Predicting we wont have that 10 percent spike for the hero, because our warmup (1 percent) will cover a much larger number of steps since the hero is at a higher step count. I think most likely scenario is the hero runs around 2 percent dropping, but up to 8 percent seems plausible bsaed on the data at 4k seqlen.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
> Thanks for sharing this work. I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. Is LatentMoE mainly motivated by reducing communication overhead at larger scales (e.g., beyond a single NVLink domain), or does it also provide benefits beyond communication optimization, such as improving model capability? Thanks!

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

comments.body: > Thanks for the detailed reply! I have a few follow-up questions after looking through some of the previous Marin experiments. 1. MAI Thinking makes their dense layers only have num_neurons = hidden_dim, which is roughly 3x smaller than normal. This to me a is a bit awkward at first glance because attn is still full capacity every layer. So the normal behavior of attention fetch info, mlp process it is a bit imbalanced (of course if one has data that an idea is good, that it seeming awkward doesn't matter, but it made me more hesitant to spend the time collecting that data instead of working on other things). At very small scale if I do an exact active:total replica (dense 3x width hidden instead of 1x), I get same quality and 20% better MFU than our baseline. We never ended up doing large scale ablation here, since I was more worried about token dropping dynamics. Also the way we are using jax scan makes it a awkward to have different behavior per layer. I am less optimistic about alternating dense/moe long term, because with mature mixture-of-kittens kernels the MFU hit of MoE is probably not that high anyways. 2. Hmm I separately saw some early positive results from Inkling relative position embedding that gave lower loss. But our kernel was not quite fast enough to justify. And perhaps more importantly, the kernel was a bit buggy if I changed sliding window length. I think it should be good on global layers too, since its limited to just the most recent X (512 or 1024) positions. I am more bullish on relative position embedding + MLA. Since MLA has very janky approach to RoPE, which requires replicating 64 head dims across every head. Relative position embedding fixes this. Have to be a bit careful with ablations here because at very small scale RoPE on global looks much better than NoPE on global. (but this fades with scale) 3. So initial AdamH on embed looked good. But later I did learning rate sweep, and if LR was 40% too high, was seeing grad spikes up to 20. I think what was happening (guessing) was rare tokens were having their norm driven to near zero, and then getting massive grad when they finally ended up in the batch. (we have rms_norm on embed that will apply high growth multiplier to small vocab embeds) Dont want any features in the model that require perfectly optimal hypers. So reverted it.

comments.author: MythosAd
comments.body:
Thanks, this is really helpful.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. With a fixed local window, the relative-position range never changes as context grows, while global attention stays purely content-addressed. I agree this probably needs larger-scale ablations to judge properly.

comments.author: yonromai
comments.body:
🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Actionable as a design proposal, not a PR.** This is a new CI-triggered deploy capability touching production infra with real trigger/safety design choices (which services, what triggers a redeploy, rollback), so posting analysis + proposed approach for review rather than a unilateral PR.

# Research

Both services already have mature deploy CLIs; what's missing is a CI job that runs them after a build/test passes. There's already a working precedent for CI-driven deploys with GCP auth.

- **finelog** deploys to a GCE VM running `ghcr.io/marin-community/finelog:latest`; restart re-pulls the image. Safe path with health-check + rollback exists.
- **ducky** is an always-on Iris TPU job; redeploy is an idempotent `--keep` watchdog submit that needs a controller tunnel.
- CI already does this pattern for the Iris controller (GCP SA auth, ephemeral OS Login SSH, run the CLI), triggered by cron + manual — no `workflow_run`-on-success deploy exists anywhere.

**Relevant code**
- [`iris-dev-restart.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/iris-dev-restart.yaml) — existing CI deploy pattern to copy (SA auth + OS Login + CLI restart)
- [`finelog/scripts/safe_deploy.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/scripts/safe_deploy.py) — `rollout`/`rollback` with health check; digest cached for rollback
- [`finelog/deploy/_gcp.py#L189`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/src/finelog/deploy/_gcp.py#L189) — `gcp_restart()` (`finelog deploy restart marin`)
- [`ducky/deploy.py#L67`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/ducky/src/ducky/deploy.py#L67) — `submit_ducky()`; `ducky deploy --cluster marin --keep`, auto-tunnels, region-pinned TPU job
- [`ops-docker-images.yaml#L100-L109`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/ops-docker-images.yaml#L100) — builds/pushes `finelog:latest` (weekly + dispatch); the natural upstream to gate finelog redeploy

# Proposed approach (design)

Add one deploy workflow per service, cloning the `iris-dev-restart.yaml` scaffold (checkout → `google-github-actions/auth` with `IRIS_CI_GCP_SA_KEY` → ephemeral OS Login SSH → run CLI → remove key). As services multiply, factor the auth+OS-Login boilerplate into a composite action under `.github/actions/` so each new service is ~15 lines. Both start with `workflow_dispatch` so they can be exercised manually before any auto-trigger is armed.

**finelog** — trigger via `workflow_run` on **Ops - Docker Images** completing successfully (that's what publishes `:latest`; restarting on merges that don't rebuild the image is pointless). Deploy step uses `safe_deploy.py rollout marin`, not raw `deploy restart`, so a bad image auto-rolls-back on health-check failure. This is genuinely small and low-risk.

**ducky** — heavier: needs a controller tunnel and submits a TPU job, and `--keep` is a no-op when the job is already healthy (only picks up new code on job restart). Suggest a separate, later workflow (or scheduled `--keep` watchdog) gated on `Ducky - Unit` success on `main`; worth its own discussion before wiring.

**Open questions for reviewers:**
1. Trigger model — `workflow_run` on the upstream build/test, or `push: branches:[main]` with `paths:` scoped to the service dir? I lean `workflow_run` so we only deploy artifacts CI actually validated.
2. Redeploy cadence — event-driven per merge, or keep it a daily scheduled refresh like `iris-dev-restart`? Per-merge finelog restarts are cheap; per-merge ducky TPU-job churn may not be desirable.
3. Should finelog redeploy always go through `safe_deploy.py` (rollback) — I assume yes.

If the trigger model + safety story above is agreed, I'll open the finelog workflow first (small, self-contained) and follow with ducky separately. cc @rjpower

issues.author: hammer
issues.body:
The [Arcee Trinity Large Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17004) in Section 3.2 Data Preparation defines a metric, Batch Heterogeneity, (BatchHet), that tracks the difference between the maximum microbatch loss and the average loss for each training step, and claim that this metric correlates strongly with gradient norm instability. They note that, as models grow larger, their step-to-step data efficiency tends to increase, and hypothesize that makes them more vulnerable to the step-to-step fluctuations in the data distribution, which causes training instability as models grow larger.

They introduce a method, the Random Sequential Document Buffer (RSDB), to reduce this metric. I'm not sure that method is useful for us as I don't believe we do on-the-fly tokenization. 

Should we track this metric? Given some of the [spikes](https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1375005693899309126/1479363883813830717) we saw with Delphi that were related to bad data, I have been having bouts of anxiety about some weird data-related training instability hit late in a hero run due to unfortunate sampling packing bad data together in unforeseen ways and have been thinking about how we could mitigate that risk. Adding this metric, creating data that causes it to spike, and developing methods to reduce it even in the face of bad data seems potentially interesting?

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
## TL;DR

A 49,152-token per-turn cap reduced `length` stops in the first temperature-1.0 training batch to 793/8,192 responses (9.7%). The 32,768-token arm had 1,038/8,192 (12.7%); the 16,384-token arm had 1,510/8,192 (18.4%). After two optimizer updates, the 32K and 48K arms each had 35 positive task outcomes on 99 shared validation prompts. We selected 48K for the longer follow-up because reducing training length stops was the primary goal. The comparison is exploratory: two updates and 99–100 validation prompts per arm do not establish long-run model quality.

## Description

Snowball 67B A2B Datakit SFT RLVR responses sometimes ended for length before a final answer. Three controlled arms used 16,384, 32,768, or 49,152 generated tokens per turn with a 65,536-token total request window. Each started from the same checkpoint, trained for two updates on 512 prompts per update with 16 responses per prompt, and evaluated before training and after each update. Training used temperature 1.0; validation used temperature 0.0. The generated-budget fraction changed with the cap, as documented in the frozen configs.

## Goal and result

The goal was to reduce training length stops while retaining reward variance within prompt groups. The second training batch had 396, 429, and 433 informative groups out of 512 for the 16K, 32K, and 48K arms. On the 99 common final validation prompts, positive task outcomes were 28, 35, and 35; length stops were 14, 13, and 10. The 32K and 48K arms shared 26 positive prompts, with nine unique positives in each. The 48K first training batch generated 70.20 million response tokens, 18% above the 32K batch.

A `length` stop may reflect the per-turn cap or the remaining total request window. The full report defines the metrics and covers per-domain outcomes, verifier status, and limitations.

## Artifacts

- [Release report](https://gist.github.com/penfever/e8a9cad2e78cd503ed988711f758367e)
- [Raw numeric evaluation records, domain summaries, training batches, and durable archive manifest](https://gist.github.com/penfever/f1602e1d923650644be5cdf1f987d5ee)
- [Frozen sweep configs and launch code](https://gist.github.com/penfever/e05a6e78953d06861d2a32e9b4b99644)
- W&B: [16K](https://wandb.ai/nyu-dice-lab/snowball-ultra-rlvr/runs/lucyb57j), [32K](https://wandb.ai/nyu-dice-lab/snowball-ultra-rlvr/runs/vlw8hz57), [48K](https://wandb.ai/nyu-dice-lab/snowball-ultra-rlvr/runs/u2a35ai1)

The data gist lists ten SHA-256-identified evaluation archives in CoreWeave object storage, including an older baseline. Full archives require Marin credentials. W&B marks these completed trainer runs `crashed`, so the release uses the archived evaluations and structured trainer logs as its source.

## Decision log

- Selected 48K per turn for the follow-up run. It had fewer training length stops than 32K and the same aggregate final validation positive count after two updates.
- Keep the existing 80 policy and 48 rollout GPUs. A larger total request window requires separate serving and memory validation.

## Conclusion

The three-arm sweep is complete and its raw numbers, configs, and report are preserved above. The longer run will test whether the 48K setting maintains useful training signal and holdout quality over more updates.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
In latentMoE, we can try initializing the up/down projections as semi-orthogonal matrices and either:

A: using an orthogonality-preserving optimizer such as the one introduced in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218 to update them
or
B: freezing them, keeping them semi-orthogonal and not updating them at all, while relying the rest of the NN to adapt

Rationale: up/down projections in latentMoE are themselves small, shared by all experts of the same layer, therefore not really having the capability to do meaningful computation for the whole NN. We should see them as information-preserving maps instead, and worry more about gradient pathology/distortion, rather than the potential loss of the degree of freedom/expressivity by using semi-orthogonal matrices.
Also if we take the "no meaningful computation" hypothesis really seriously, option B should only have negligible performance degradation compared to A. And if we use B, no new optimizer and no new hyperparameter tuning are needed.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: 🤖 Second intake test (end-to-end on main, scheduled run): this comment should be copied into #9451 within a few minutes of its 👍, then get a 🚀. Not a research suggestion.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.

Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.

But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:

1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting

And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.

The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Attention residuals q embedding:
In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from

exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))

into

exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))

q_e should be initialized as all 0.

Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
After #7064, every controller issues its tokens under its cluster `name`. The control-plane verifier also accepts the old generic issuer `iris` so that worker tokens minted before a cluster was named keep verifying across the restart that renames it.

Those tokens live for `WORKER_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS` (30 days). Once 30 days have passed since the **marin controller restart** that renames it, every pre-rename token has passed its `exp`, and removing the acceptance is provably a no-op. A worker VM created shortly before the cut still holds a valid legacy token, which is why the window is a full TTL rather than a shorter rollout period.

To remove, in `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/auth.py`:

- drop `_LEGACY_ISSUER` from the `JwksVerifier` issuer map in `_build_jwt_token_manager`
- drop the `cluster_name or _LEGACY_ISSUER` fallback (`name` is required by `validate_config`)
- delete the constant and the tests that pin its behaviour (`test_worker_token_minted_before_the_cluster_was_named_still_verifies`, `test_legacy_issuer_still_requires_this_controllers_key`)

The federation plane is unaffected: its verifier keys each peer by its own name and never accepted `iris`, which `test_legacy_issuer_is_not_accepted_on_the_federation_plane` pins.

Done when:

- [ ] Register a pinned official release in the Atlas with source links, task counts, and applicable license information.
- [ ] Run the standard sampled quality review using the native Harbor verifier, preserving solver, verifier, and judge evidence.
- [ ] If the source qualifies as Good, run the current Atlas difficulty protocol across its Small, Large, and Hosted models on the same task sample. Record model identities, settings, sample selection, solve counts, and infrastructure failures separately.
- [ ] Make the source and dated review results visible in the Atlas, and link the implementation PR and evidence here.

- Activation, weighting, and buffer fusions: inspect SwiGLU forward/backward, route-weight application, and dispatch/combine staging copies. Benchmark opportunities that remove an intermediate allocation or memory pass after checking what our current kernels already fuse.

comments.body:
🤖 # Research

Effort: low (pinned source and linked results; no GB200 run).

At the pinned Hero revision, EP64 uses d6144, latent/intermediate 3072, E384/top-8, and six local experts in three waves; the weight-gradient benchmark's default 301,466 rows and three groups does not establish this recipe's accepted per-wave shape. QuACK already fuses the gate/up forward GEMM with SwiGLU and covers all six grouped GEMMs; ragged dispatch uses one gather, and combine has a fused weighted-sum path. OLMo-core `a800c06` exposes grouped-MM output and input-gradient buffers, valid-prefix SwiGLU forward/backward, and packed shared-expert projections, whose benefit at Marin's JAX boundary is unmeasured. [#9077](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9077) compared XLA/cuDNN with QuACK for another chunk, [#8311](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8311) covers fused EP, and [PR #9481](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9481) covers transport overlap; no open PR targets an OLMo-core or SwiGLU comparison.

**Relevant code**
- [Hero shape](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ae9115497494655baac21dd03a61d205ac73ab2/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py#L85-L115) — model, routing, waves.

- [Ragged transport](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ae9115497494655baac21dd03a61d205ac73ab2/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ragged_all_to_all.py#L155-L203) — dispatch and combine.

- [OLMo shared experts](https://github.com/allenai/olmo-core/blob/a800c06edcec8e4652de2f80fe0ea572d689fcc3/src/olmo_core/nn/moe/v2/shared_experts.py#L122-L162) — packed up/gate projection.

# Proposed Fix

1. Pin a current Marin commit, OLMo-core `a800c06`, JAX/jaxlib, PyTorch, cuDNN, cuBLAS, QuACK, CUDA, GB200 allocation, and the [Hero recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ae9115497494655baac21dd03a61d205ac73ab2/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/hero_recipe.py#L31-L47). Freeze one checkpoint and batch/assignment trace for all matched arms.
2. Extend [`bench_grouped_wgrad.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ae9115497494655baac21dd03a61d205ac73ab2/lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grouped_wgrad.py#L141-L199) to cover forward, activation-gradient, weight-gradient, and complete MLP forward/backward at each observed wave shape. Compare shipped tuned QuACK, the relevant XLA path, and OLMo's BF16 grouped-MM path; verify PyTorch selects its CUDA fast path rather than its host-offset fallback. Use identical seeded-normal operands (record the seed) and checkpoint-derived offsets, at least five warmups and 30 measured repetitions per variant. Report kernel time separately from the complete operator including layout conversion, output-buffer writes, and JAX↔PyTorch boundary costs, plus peak memory and forward/gradient error against the same float32 reference.
3. Profile-gate the smaller candidates. Compare [OLMo's valid-prefix SwiGLU backward](https://github.com/allenai/olmo-core/blob/a800c06edcec8e4652de2f80fe0ea572d689fcc3/src/olmo_core/kernels/swiglu.py#L67-L119) with Marin's compiled backward only if the trace shows a separate pass or allocation. Benchmark one packed up/gate projection and batched down projection for the two [separate shared MLP calls](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ae9115497494655baac21dd03a61d205ac73ab2/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1187-L1192); retain separate logical parameter leaves and verify per-matrix MuonH updates.
4. Score repeated post-warmup steps without profiling overhead; record full-step throughput, loss, forward/backward error, dropped assignments, and peak memory, with W&B/XProf links. For any new communication-overlap candidate, compare unsplit, sequential chunks, and overlapped chunks under the same routing trace; reuse PR #9481's results when the configuration matches.
5. Post an adopt/defer/reject table here with exact commands, versions, seeds/checkpoint, timing boundaries, repetition distributions, and profile/run links. Adopt only a repeatable full-step gain above control variance with matching loss, drops, and optimizer behavior. Keep MXFP8 and routing changes in separate follow-ups.

`ShellSimEnvironment.download_dir()` converts its target with `pathlib.Path`. Harbor can supply a remote `S3Path` for a trial log directory. `Path(S3Path(...))` raises `TypeError`, so Harbor cannot collect agent logs after a trial error.

The Snowball coding-expert smoke in #9528 confirmed this after the agent endpoint returned HTTP 400:

```text
File "shellbox/backends/shellsim/environment.py", line 146, in download_dir
    target = Path(target_dir)
TypeError: argument should be a str or an os.PathLike object where __fspath__ returns a str, not 'S3Path'
```

This secondary failure removes the useful agent log and makes the first failure harder to diagnose.

Support Harbor's remote path objects in `download_file()` and `download_dir()`. Download from ShellSim to a local temporary path, then copy the result to the remote target. Keep the current direct path for local targets.

The temporary workaround for #9528 implements this staging path in Shellbox. Tests must cover a non-`pathlib.Path` target without access to live object storage.

# Research

`ShellSimEnvironment.download_file()` and `download_dir()` convert every target with `Path(...)`, while `ShellSimMachine.download()` requires a local path. Harbor supplies an `S3Path` for remote trial logs, so conversion raises before the logs can be copied. Harbor's Daytona adapter already stages remote downloads locally and streams them to `UPath` targets.

**Relevant code**
- [`environment.py#L137-L149`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/shellsim/environment.py#L137-L149) — target conversion
- [`machine.py#L143-L162`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/shellsim/machine.py#L143-L162) — local download contract
- [`environment.py#L179-L218`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/6f94f2237224869a49c249a737d701147afc33b6/src/harbor/environments/daytona/environment.py#L179-L218) — remote copy pattern

# Proposed Fix

`Harbor trial → ShellSimEnvironment.download_dir() → Path(S3Path) → TypeError`. Keep direct downloads for local targets; for remote `UPath` targets, download to a temporary local path and stream the file or directory tree to the target off the event loop. Cover both methods with an in-memory `UPath` target, without object storage access.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
Faster transformer gives us better quality results than fast-text, but running on CPU it's too slow to use in practice. On TPU, this shouldn't be the case: a v6e operating at full capacity would be able to run on all param

Let's iterate on some faster transformer designs and inference parameters (batch size, max tokens per doc) and setup a Zephyr job for 100M -> 1B token datakit quality runs and check how fast we can get this.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 This is a research/benchmarking task (iterate on model + inference params, stand up a 100M→1B-token Zephyr quality run, measure throughput), not a self-contained bug fix — so per the agent workflow I'm posting analysis for a human to drive, not opening a PR.

# Research

The pooled fast-transformer classifier is **already TPU-capable**: the forward pass is jitted equinox/JAX, casts matmuls to bf16 for the MXU, and `predict()` shards each batch across all chips of a v6e slice via a data-parallel mesh, auto-shrinking batch size to a 262k-token activation budget so long context doesn't OOM one chip. What is *not* TPU-wired is the **production Zephyr quality stage**: `score_normalized()` requests `ResourceConfig(cpu=2, ram="8g")` and runs under `InlineRunner`, i.e. workers land on CPU boxes and JAX falls back to the CPU backend. That's the "too slow on CPU" the issue describes — the code path exists, it's just never scheduled onto TPU.

**Relevant code**
- [`score.py#L58-L63`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/datakit/cluster/quality/fast_transformer/score.py#L58-L63) — quality stage `BATCH_SIZE=512`, **CPU-only** `WORKER_RESOURCES`
- [`score.py#L172-L189`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/datakit/cluster/quality/fast_transformer/score.py#L172-L189) — the Zephyr pipeline (`window(BATCH_SIZE)` → `_predict_batch` → split-writer), InlineRunner keeps the model warm per worker
- [`inference.py#L25-L34`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/datakit/cluster/quality/fast_transformer/inference.py#L25-L34) — data-parallel mesh over `jax.devices()`; [`#L43-L67`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/datakit/cluster/quality/fast_transformer/inference.py#L43-L67) — token-budget batch sizing (`_PREDICT_TOKEN_BUDGET=262144`)
- [`model.py#L44-L56`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/datakit/cluster/quality/fast_transformer/model.py#L44-L56) — `FastTransformerConfig` (width/depth/`pool_window`); [`#L76-L95`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/datakit/cluster/quality/fast_transformer/model.py#L76-L95) — `flops_per_token()` (held under ~1M)
- [`scorer.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/datakit/cluster/quality/fast_transformer/scorer.py) — `score_bme` whole-doc begin/middle/end windowing (deployed `MAX_TOKENS=512`)

# Proposed approach (for review before implementation)

1. **Schedule the stage on TPU.** Thread a TPU `ResourceConfig` (v6e slice) into `score_normalized`'s `worker_resources` instead of the CPU default; confirm workers get JAX TPU devices and `data_parallel_shardings()` sees all chips. This alone should be the bulk of the speedup and is the first thing to measure.
2. **Sweep inference params for throughput (docs/sec/chip).** `BATCH_SIZE` and `max_tokens` (512 → 1024) against the 262k token budget, and `pool_window` / `embed_dim` / `num_layers` / `num_heads` in `FastTransformerConfig` — the pooled arch amortizes cost ~`pool_window`×, so there's headroom to widen the model at fixed wall-clock. Watch recompiles: each new padded sequence length triggers a jit compile.
3. **Stand up the 100M→1B-token run.** Point the reference-pipeline quality step at a corpus slice sized to ~100M then ~1B tokens, record docs/sec, tokens/sec/chip, and MXU utilization, and check quality-bucket calibration still holds at the larger token budget.

Open questions for the issue author (@rjpower): which v6e topology to target, which corpus/source to benchmark on, and whether "faster transformer designs" means tuning the existing pooled arch or also trying new architectures. Happy to prototype step 1 (the TPU resource wiring) as a small PR if that's the desired starting point.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Milestone 1 — plan (researched + peer-reviewed).** Benchmarking the pooled fast-transformer quality classifier on v6e TPU via a **Zephyr pipeline** on the `marin` cluster (`europe-west4-a`).

**Central finding from the code:** the deployed config is **~55.5K FLOPs/token** (28.4M FLOPs per 512-token window). A `v6e-4` (4 chips × 918 TFLOP/s bf16) has a compute ceiling of **~66 G tokens/s** at 100% MXU — orders of magnitude above any host feed rate. So the forward pass is essentially free and **throughput is host-bound** (HF tokenization + the Python token-remap/pack loop), not device-bound. That reframes the whole exercise: to actually use the TPU we must stop the host from starving it.

**Design — three measurements, all as Zephyr jobs:**
- **A. Monolithic** `score_normalized` flipped onto TPU workers (minimal-migration reference; host tokenization blocks the forward).
- **B. Split pipeline** (the fix): a CPU fleet tokenizes + packs `[N,512]` token-ids, then a TPU fleet runs the batched forward + window→doc reduction + calibration. Both stages stay `map_shard`-per-file so the datakit basename/row-order join contract is preserved. This decouples the CPU bottleneck from the TPU so each scales independently.
- **C. fasttext** on the same corpus slice (CPU) for an apples-to-apples throughput/$/quality comparison. Plus a forward-only microbenchmark for the device upper bound.

**Comparison anchors:** recorded quality is **FT Spearman 0.69 vs fasttext 0.44** (5,010 oracle labels; commit `3a846e3e38`); **no throughput number exists for either** — generating those fresh. Deliverable will report tokens/sec, per-stage breakdown, and a **10T-corpus projection** (chip-hours / $ / wall-clock) for FT-on-TPU vs fasttext-on-CPU.

Plan was peer-reviewed (codex, 13 findings incorporated: per-shard join-contract safety, no false "MXU saturation" claim, full-host TPU workers, real-slice vocab remap, three reported rates, identical token accounting). Executing now; will post per-stage numbers as they land.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Milestone 2 — device ceiling measured on v6e (forward-only microbenchmark).**

Ran the pooled fast-transformer forward on a **v6e-4** (4 chips, `europe-west4-a`) with pre-tokenized resident batches, warm compile, 32 async launches before sync — i.e. the *device upper bound*, deliberately excluding host tokenization:

| global batch | tokens/s | tokens/s/chip | MXU util |
|---|---|---|---|
| 512 | 377 M | 94 M | 0.57% |
| **2048** | **670 M** | **167 M** | **1.01%** |
| 8192 | 635 M | 159 M | 0.96% |
| 32768 | 596 M | 149 M | 0.90% |
| 65536 | 579 M | 145 M | 0.88% |

**The forward pass uses ~1% of the v6e's MXU** and tops out around **670 M window-tokens/s per v6e-4** (~167 M/chip), peaking at batch ~2048 and regressing slightly beyond (dispatch/HBM bound, not compute). At 55.5K FLOPs/token this tiny pooled model simply can't fill the MXU — so on TPU the classifier forward is essentially free, and end-to-end throughput is gated by **host-side tokenization**, exactly as predicted. That's what the split pipeline (CPU tokenize fleet → TPU forward fleet) is designed to exploit.

Corpus for the end-to-end runs: `normalized/nemotron_cc_v2/high_quality` (real CommonCrawl web text, 47% of docs long enough for 3 begin/middle/end windows). Building the scorer and running the split + fasttext comparison next.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Fast-transformer quality classifier on v6e: throughput and scaling**

A single v6e-4 scores the pooled fast-transformer quality classifier at **~18,000 docs/s** (a warm 190K-doc shard in ~10.5s). Per-VM throughput is independent, so a 10T-token corpus (~11.1B docs) takes **~2.7 h on 64 v6e-4** (~0.7 h on 256), using preemptible TPUs. Throughput is set by host work — the forward runs at ~1% MXU — so the pipeline is built to parallelize the host, and the model can grow ~10–20× in FLOPs/token before the forward becomes the limit. Tokenization is the largest host cost: replacing the deployed SentencePiece tokenizer with a tiktoken BPE (`o200k_base`) raises throughput to **~26,600 docs/s** at matched classifier quality.

## Setup

- **Model**: the deployed pooled fast-transformer (`embed_dim=256, layers=2, heads=4, pool_window=64, max_tokens=512`), tokenizer `intfloat/multilingual-e5-small`, begin/middle/end windowing (~1.94 windows/doc), 55.5K FLOPs/token. A config-faithful scorer with random weights (real vocab remap from a corpus slice); throughput depends only on config, vocab size, and token-length distribution, so it is weight-independent.
- **Corpus**: `nemotron_cc_v2/high_quality` slice, `europe-west4` (3,611 chars/doc mean, 189.6K docs/shard, 396 MB text column/shard).
- **Hardware**: v6e-4 (`ct6e-standard-4t`) = 4 chips + 180-vCPU host, marin cluster, `europe-west4-a`. Zephyr-on-Iris, one shard per worker, warm JAX under `InlineRunner`.

## Method

The forward-only device ceiling (microbenchmark, resident batches) is ~670 M window-tok/s at ~1% MXU, above any achievable host feed rate. The pipeline parallelizes the three host costs:

- **Read**: each shard's ~11 parquet row groups are read concurrently (`id`/`text` columns, arrow-native), reducing the 396 MB read from ~15s to ~2.7s.
- **Tokenize**: a fork process pool (96 workers) tokenizes off the GIL and returns packed blocks through shared memory.
- **Forward**: a stager thread issues `device_put` for upcoming blocks so the H2D transfer overlaps the current forward and reduction.

## Parameter sweep

Warm per-shard cost over `tok_procs` × `device_batch` (before the stager change):

| tok_procs | device_batch | warm compute | warm/shard | warm docs/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 96 | 4096 | 5.1s | 10.6s | ~17,900 |
| 96 | 8192 | 7.6s | 12.9s | ~14,700 |
| 48 | 8192 | 8.3s | 13.6s | ~13,800 |
| 96 | 16384 | 13.2s | 18.7s | ~10,200 |
| 48 | 4096 | ~7.0s | ~12.6s | ~15,000 |

Doubling the fork pool (48→96) reduced compute 7.0s→5.1s. Increasing `device_batch` increased it: a larger batch produces fewer, larger tokenize tasks, which underuse the pool. Adding the stager thread reduced compute a further 5.1s→4.7s. Selected configuration: 96 procs, `device_batch` 4096 — warm shard read 2.7s + compute 4.7s + write 3.1s = ~10.5s.

## Throughput

| path | hardware | warm docs/s | quality (Spearman)† |
|---|---|---|---|
| fast (this work) | 1× v6e-4 | ~18,000 | ~0.69 |
| fast, tiktoken `o200k_base` | 1× v6e-4 | ~26,600 | 0.70 |
| fast, 4 workers | 4× v6e-4 (16 chips) | ~18,000/VM → ~72,000 aggregate | ~0.69 |
| fast, first working version | 1× v6e-4 | 8,345 | ~0.69 |
| fast, single-tokenizer | 1× v6e-4 | 2,573 | ~0.69 |
| CPU-only | 32 vCPU | ~1,600 | ~0.69 |
| fasttext (deployed baseline) | 32 vCPU | 6,122 | ~0.44 |

Per-VM throughput is unchanged from 1 to 4 workers (each has its own host, chips, and output shards; the GCS read did not degrade), so aggregate throughput scales linearly. The CPU-only path is limited by the forward, which is not free on CPU.

The same harness runs unchanged on CoreWeave 8×H100 (`--accelerator H100x8`, reading the corpus and scorer from CoreWeave S3): **~22,700 docs/s** warm (read 2.8s + compute 4.1s + write 1.4s). It is slightly faster than v6e-4 because the CoreWeave object store writes the output shard in ~1.4s versus ~3.1s on GCS; the workload is host-bound on either accelerator.

†The throughput harness uses random weights; the Spearman column is a trained model's held-out oracle rank correlation. The tiktoken figure is a controlled retrain (below); the SentencePiece rows carry the deployed model's evaluation, and fasttext its own.

## Tokenizer

Tokenization is the largest host cost, so the tokenizer is the main lever on throughput. Swapping the deployed SentencePiece tokenizer (`multilingual-e5-small`, 250K vocab) for a tiktoken BPE (`o200k_base`) tokenizes ~6× faster per core and roughly halves the compute phase. A warm shard then splits read 2.4s + compute 2.4s + write 2.1s ≈ 7.0s (**~26,600 docs/s**), with the three phases balanced — the parquet read and score write dominate, so further tokenizer speedups return little.

A controlled retrain (same architecture, data, seed, and eval split; only the tokenizer changed) gives held-out oracle Spearman **0.700** for `o200k_base` versus **0.695** for `multilingual-e5-small` — matched within noise. The tiktoken tokenizer is thus ~1.5× faster end to end at equal quality.

## Scaling to 10T tokens

11.07 B docs at 903 corpus-tok/doc:

| VMs (v6e-4) | chips | wall-clock |
|---|---|---|
| 16 | 64 | ~10.7 h |
| 64 | 256 | ~2.7 h |
| 256 | 1024 | ~0.7 h |

## Model size

The forward takes ~0.5s of the ~10.5s shard and scales ~linearly with FLOPs/token:

| growth in FLOPs/token | effect |
|---|---|
| ~8× (~0.5 M/tok) | forward equals tokenization |
| ~20× (~1.1 M/tok) | forward equals the host critical path — the TPU becomes the limit |
| ~100× (~5.5 M/tok) | forward saturates the MXU |

A model up to ~10–20× larger in FLOPs/token (e.g. ~4× wider or ~10 layers deeper) runs at the same throughput.

*Harness: `experiments/datakit/cluster/quality/fast_transformer/tpu_bench/` (#7191).*
