issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
PR #9626 adds a bounded artifact graph for the post-training recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop. The graph uses `TaskSpec`, TaskCompendium Parquet, `ShellboxRolloutEngine`, Marin artifact steps, and real grading. The policy, task generation, task filter, failure analysis, and training stages use deterministic stubs.

Replace the stubs with one small-model path that runs the full loop on Iris. The run must start from a pinned checkpoint and a held-out evaluation set. It must generate new tasks from observed failures, train new model weights, and evaluate the new checkpoint on the same held-out set.

Related open work:

- #7098: run post-training experiments from Marin
- #9612: use one rollout engine for `TaskSpec` rollouts
- #9122: define the task environment contract
- #7799: build a normalized and versioned post-training data pool
- #8089: establish the cold-start SFT recipe
- #6503: run configured evaluations and publish their results
- marin-community/MarinSkyRL#809: define the supported RL training contract
- [Post-training project](https://github.com/orgs/marin-community/projects/5): draft items for problem generation and error-mode identification

Done when:

- One versioned configuration identifies the base checkpoint, task sources, held-out evaluation set, generator, trainer, and maximum round count.
- The initial evaluation stores graded rollouts and metrics before task generation.
- Failure analysis converts failed rollouts into task prompts without copying held-out answers into training data.
- The problem generator writes verifiable `TaskSpec` records, and the task filter records accepted and rejected tasks.
- The shared rollout engine generates and grades training rollouts.
- The trainer updates real model weights and exports a checkpoint that the next evaluation can load.
- The final evaluation uses the original held-out set and records a comparison with the initial evaluation.
- Every stage records immutable inputs, outputs, and versions. A failed run can continue from completed artifacts.
- A small-model smoke run completes at least one feedback round on Iris and links its artifacts from this issue.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

[#9626](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9626) defines a bounded artifact graph, but its policy is a capability list and its analysis, generator, filter, and trainer are stubs. Its rollout records retain only four fields. [#9623](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9623) supplies the shared TaskCompendium rollout engine, and its [Qwen3-4B Iris smoke](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9612#issuecomment-5933580920) produced one optimizer step and a loadable HF export. Both PRs remain open and own the graph and rollout engine foundations.

**Relevant code**
- [`pipeline.py#L175-L280`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9774e2cd1b4acac2b8b1524e710b217a700fcc22/experiments/post_training/baby_rsi/pipeline.py#L175-L280) — bounded artifact dependencies.
- [`interfaces.py#L23-L69`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9774e2cd1b4acac2b8b1524e710b217a700fcc22/experiments/post_training/baby_rsi/interfaces.py#L23-L69) — dummy policy and reduced rollout records.
- [`dummy.py#L1-L30`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9774e2cd1b4acac2b8b1524e710b217a700fcc22/experiments/post_training/baby_rsi/dummy.py#L1-L30) — replacement boundaries.
- [`task_rollouts.py#L201-L247`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/96936d8f7762c3cea613ff2353e3bde0f656205b/experiments/post_training/task_rollouts.py#L201-L247) — working Qwen3-4B trainer configuration.
- [`skyrl.py#L212-L225`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L212-L225) — exported checkpoint and evaluation adapter.

# Proposed Fix

## Design

Extend the #9626 graph with one versioned `BabyRsiConfig`: `Qwen/Qwen3-4B@1cfa9a7` as the base policy, a pinned TaskCompendium math source with disjoint held-out IDs, a pinned generator model and prompt revision, the #9623 SkyRL trainer recipe, seed, artifact prefix, and caps of one round, 32 held-out tasks, 32 accepted new tasks, and one optimizer step. Select and freeze the held-out IDs before the baseline run. Use the same TaskSpec Parquet artifact, generation settings, and task IDs for the baseline and final evaluation; record per-task grades and aggregate pass counts. Mark a run with no baseline failures inconclusive.

Replace the in-memory `PolicyState` and reduced `RolloutBuffer` with artifact references to the policy export and full graded `RolloutData`. Add an `ArtifactSkyRLModel` input adapter so the exported `SkyRLModel.policy_export_uri` from round *n* can initialize round *n+1*; `ArtifactHfModel` currently expects a Levanter checkpoint. Keep the existing Marin artifact fingerprints and write a manifest for each stage with the config revision, input artifact identities, task/verifier versions, model revision, seed, and output paths. This lets a retry reuse completed stages while rejecting mismatched inputs.

Failure analysis should consume only public task metadata, the model response, grade, and failure category. Its output is a capability-level `TaskPrompt`; the generator must not receive the held-out Parquet, task text, expected answers, or private verifier payload. Adapt the existing [math curriculum generator](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9774e2cd1b4acac2b8b1524e710b217a700fcc22/experiments/post_training/baby_rsi/generation.py) to produce new TaskSpecs with independently checked answers. Persist every proposed task and an accept/reject decision with a reason; reject malformed or unverifiable tasks and exact or normalized duplicates of held-out and accepted training tasks. Feed accepted TaskSpecs to `ShellboxRolloutEngine`, retain its graded trajectories and failures, and pass only valid training records to the SkyRL trainer. Report the paired baseline/final results even if the score falls.

## Sequence and validation

1. Land or rebase on #9623 and #9626, then pin the exact revisions of the TaskCompendium source, generator, SkyRL runtime, and base checkpoint in one config. Keep the RSI implementation on a follow-up branch so it does not duplicate either open PR.
2. Add behavior tests for held-out answer isolation, accepted/rejected task audit rows, artifact invalidation on changed inputs, and loading the previous round's exported weights. Exercise baseline → generation → training → final evaluation with a tiny local fixture before Iris.
3. Run the one-round Qwen3-4B smoke on Iris with the proven 16-H100 topology from #9623. Publish the initial graded rollouts, filter decisions, training rollouts, optimizer step, HF export/reload evidence, final graded rollouts, and comparison here. Preserve a failed or negative result with its artifact links.

## Risks and open decision

The current [curriculum generator](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9774e2cd1b4acac2b8b1524e710b217a700fcc22/experiments/post_training/baby_rsi/README.md#L37-L64) checks a generated answer with an independent solve but can still accept a shared mistake; the smoke must keep those audit rows and grade training rollouts with TaskCompendium. Which pinned math cohort should be the held-out set? I would start with a fixed TaskTrove math subset after [#9587](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9587) lands, because it already targets TaskSpec conversion and keeps this first loop within one verifier family.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
We want to introduce a workflow to allow external submissions to the Marin/Iris cluster.

This will allow a broader set of users to contribute to Marin experiments and for us to validate without requiring manual intervention to check out branches and execute experiments manually. It also encourages us to better "package" experiments, so that, for example, the top-level experiment file encapsulates all Iris client operations, instead of the current approach which requires users to run `uv run iris` to boot applications (a common area of complaints).

As a incremental step, let's adjust our existing Grug/Dupekit examples to handle the Iris launching themselves, and add a workflow for trusted users which triggers an agent to run the given experiment on an Iris cluster.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue, AGENTS.md, fix-issue and author-pr skills
- [x] Survey current grug/datakit launch flow and existing GitHub workflows
- [x] Decide scope: multi-module feature + workflow + design choices — too large for an auto-PR
- [x] Post research + proposed approach for human review (no PR)

**Research**

Two distinct asks:

1. **Self-launching experiments** — today `python -m experiments.grug.base.launch` (or `datakit_testbed/train.py`) just builds configs; the Iris submission has to be wrapped externally by `uv run iris --cluster=marin job run --extra=cpu -- python -m experiments.X`. `train_grug` already calls [`_submit_train_job`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/defaults.py#L555-L588), which calls `current_client()`. That `current_client()` only resolves to a real cluster when an `IrisContext` is already in scope — which is what `uv run iris job run` sets up. Letting the launch script run end-to-end from a plain `python …/launch.py` means each launch needs to open its own `IrisClient.remote(...)` + `iris_ctx_scope(...)` (see [`client.py#L481-L516`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/client/client.py#L481-L516), [`client.py#L1109-L1120`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/client/client.py#L1109-L1120)) before invoking the existing entrypoint. Datakit testbed has the same shape via `executor_main` over `run_testbed_trial` steps.

2. **GitHub submission workflow** — `.github/workflows/marin-canary-ferry.yaml` already shows the GCP-auth + `.venv/bin/iris job run --no-wait` + `scripts/workflows/iris_monitor.py wait/collect` recipe for a single hard-coded experiment. `ops-claude.yaml` shows the trusted-user gate (`author_association in (OWNER, MEMBER, COLLABORATOR)`). What is missing is a parameterized workflow that accepts an experiment path (PR comment / `workflow_dispatch` input) and submits *that* experiment, gated on the same association check.

**Relevant code**
- [`experiments/grug/base/launch.py#L169-L252`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/base/launch.py#L169-L252) — current `__main__` calls `train_grug` but requires `iris job run` wrapper
- [`experiments/grug/README.md#L40-L48`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/README.md#L40-L48) — documents the current `uv run iris ... -- python -m …` boilerplate users complain about
- [`experiments/defaults.py#L555-L588`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/defaults.py#L555-L588) — `_submit_train_job` / `current_client()` dependency
- [`lib/iris/config/marin.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/config/marin.yaml) — production cluster config the workflow needs to pick up
- [`.github/workflows/marin-canary-ferry.yaml#L38-L100`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/marin-canary-ferry.yaml#L38-L100) — template for GCP auth + iris submission in CI
- [`.github/workflows/ops-claude.yaml#L17-L36`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/ops-claude.yaml#L17-L36) — `author_association` trusted-user gate
- [`scripts/workflows/iris_monitor.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/scripts/workflows/iris_monitor.py) — reusable `wait` + `collect` monitoring

**Proposed Approach (for review — not implementing yet)**

*Step 1: introduce a small `experiments/_launch.py` helper.*

```python
# experiments/_launch.py
def with_iris(fn, *, cluster: str = "marin", controller: str | None = None,
              workspace: Path | None = None) -> None:
    """Open an IrisClient + ctx and invoke fn() under it.

    Resolves controller address from IRIS_CONTROLLER_ADDRESS env var (set
    by `iris job run`) or by reading lib/iris/config/<cluster>.yaml.
    No-op if an IrisContext is already in scope — keeps `iris job run -- ...`
    backwards-compatible for the ferry workflows.
    """
```

Then each variant's `__main__` becomes:

```python
if __name__ == "__main__":
    from experiments._launch import with_iris
    with_iris(lambda: train_grug(name="grug/base-trial", launch=grug_base_launch))
```

Only the targets called out in the issue change in this increment: `experiments/grug/base/launch.py`, `experiments/grug/moe/launch.py`, and `experiments/datakit_testbed/train.py` (it already wraps `executor_main`; just gain the same `with_iris` wrap on its `__main__`). The README's "Iris cluster run" snippet collapses to `uv run python experiments/grug/base/launch.py`.

*Step 2: add `.github/workflows/ops-run-experiment.yaml`.*

- Trigger: `issue_comment` on PRs/issues with body starting `/run-experiment <path>` AND `author_association ∈ {OWNER, MEMBER, COLLABORATOR}` (mirror `ops-claude.yaml`).
- Parse the path with a tiny inline script; reject anything not under `experiments/`.
- Steps follow `marin-canary-ferry.yaml`: GCP auth → SSH key → `.venv/bin/iris --config=$IRIS_CONFIG job run --no-wait --extra=cpu -- python -m <module>` → `iris_monitor.py wait` → `iris_monitor.py collect`.
- Post status + W&B link back as a single PR comment (`gh pr comment --edit-last`).
- Reuse the existing `IRIS_CI_GCP_SA_KEY` / `IRIS_CI_GCP_SSH_KEY` secrets.

**Design questions to resolve before implementation**

1. Trust model: collaborator association is the same gate as `@claude`. Good enough for "trusted users" the issue mentions, or do we want a separate allowlist file?
2. Branch ref: the workflow should check out `github.event.issue.pull_request` head SHA for PR comments, and `main` for issue comments. Confirm both are in scope.
3. Resource cap: should we constrain `--reserve` to a per-comment allowlist (e.g. `v5p-8` only) to bound cost, similar to canary jobs?
4. Concurrency: `concurrency.group: run-experiment-${{ github.event.issue.number }}` to prevent double-submits on quick repeated comments?
5. Scope of Step 1: just the three files above, or also sweep every `experiments/*/launch.py` that has the boilerplate? The issue says "incremental step" — recommend the three.

Will not open a PR until these are answered. ~250 LOC across helper + workflow once Q1–Q5 land.

issues.author: mcwitt-agent
issues.body:
Hero training has irregular step-latency spikes and corresponding dips in `throughput/tokens_per_second`. Immediate jemalloc page purging is the dominant cause in a controlled 64-GPU reproduction and a likely cause of the checkpoint-associated production spikes. The fix remains undecided.

In the [704-GPU production run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-ragged_a2a-nccl2307-ep-step81k), 14 of 16 sampled steps longer than 20 seconds were emitted during checkpoint saves. Of 703 sampled steps, 21 fell within save intervals and had a median duration of 20.576 seconds; 677 outside saves and their following 60-second windows had a median of 16.868 seconds. The remaining five samples fell within 60 seconds after completion. This is a posthoc association from Finelog metrics, not a controlled production comparison. [Full findings, query provenance, and diagnostic links](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/438).

Reproduce:

1. Run the hero model computation and offloaded optimizer on 64 GB200 GPUs, with random initial weights and synthetic batches. Save separate immutable synthetic arrays, eight GiB per rank, through the real checkpoint serializer into one shared OCDBT store: 512 GiB per save.
2. Start with the hero allocator settings from #8550: `background_thread:true,dirty_decay_ms:0,muzzy_decay_ms:0,narenas:2`. Compare six training steps overlapping a save against no-save controls.
3. Set both decay values to `-1` on every initialized arena, including the large-allocation arena; repeat two saves, restore both values to `0`, and repeat the immediate-purge condition. The [completed diagnostic](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fmwittmann%2Fhero-model-checkpoint-purge-coord-20260915) contains the submitted command and per-rank logs. Full setup and evidence-retention limitations are in the linked findings.

| Condition | Rank-0 time for six training steps | Dirty-page purge calls, summed across 64 ranks |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| No checkpoint, three controls | 97.407 / 97.167 / 97.072 s | — |
| Immediate purging, first save | 121.732 s | 8,482,180 |
| Purging disabled, first save | 99.400 s | 0 |
| Purging disabled, second save | 97.724 s | 0 |
| Immediate purging restored, second save | 113.537 s | 8,478,046 |

Condition order was no-save, immediate, no-save, disabled, disabled, immediate, no-save. Jemalloc remained enabled throughout; no GPU profiling ran during this comparison. These totals exclude staging, allocator-setting changes, and final checkpoint synchronization. All writes finished within the six-step windows. The longest rank-0 steps were 35.715 and 22.332 seconds with immediate purging, versus 17.330 and 16.580 seconds with purging disabled. The restored immediate-purge setting brought the slowdown back.

Separate GPU traces showed increased collective waits and host launch delays, with little change in median compute or transfer time. The specific allocator lock or kernel operation delaying launches was not captured. The reproduction uses synthetic checkpoint arrays and one rack; it does not establish the cause of every production outlier.

Data-loader latency is unlikely to explain this reproduced effect: synthetic batches still produced the spikes. Production process-0 batch waits were at most 56.8 microseconds in the broader sampled interval. Other-rank or indirect loader interference remains possible. #7474 tracks a separate loader-starvation mechanism; cold-open PR #8333 was closed as deprioritized, with its successor #8465 already merged. Limiting S3 request concurrency did not provide a repeatable benefit in the full-model shared-store comparison.

Relative to the preceding no-save condition, disabling purging increased allocator-reported resident memory by a median across nodes of 64.13 GiB after the first save and 69.28 GiB after the second, summing the four ranks on each node. These are not total process-memory measurements, and two saves do not establish long-run stability. Reverting jemalloc risks the earlier checkpoint OOMs reported in [#8506](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8506#issuecomment-5381228200); #6932 documents earlier allocator retention. Finite decay and coordinated reclamation are unvalidated candidates. No production setting was changed.

Expected: checkpointing should avoid the reproduced large training slowdown while preserving checkpoint correctness and bounded host-memory usage. Any fix needs repeated-save measurements of total wall-clock training time, worst-step latency, peak host memory, and memory recovery between saves; moving pauses outside the throughput timer is insufficient.

Related: #8506 tracks hero operations; #8317 tracks steady-state ragged-EP throughput tuning. Neither is a dedicated tracker for this checkpoint-associated latency regression.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 The ten-second configuration in #9182 does not yet implement the intended treatment. The [first 64-GPU treatment](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fmwittmann%2Fhero-checkpoint-decay-10000-coord-20260916-r2) failed its startup assertion: jemalloc's dedicated large-allocation arena still reported `dirty_decay_ms:0`. No timed treatment results were produced.

CPU-only probes in the same Iris task image found a second bypass: disabling that dedicated arena with `oversize_threshold:0` still left arena 0 eagerly purging allocations larger than 8 MiB. The image reports jemalloc `5.3.0-0-g54eaed1d8b56b1aa528be3bdd1877e59c56fa90c`, aarch64, and 64 KiB pages. In [arena.c](https://github.com/jemalloc/jemalloc/blob/5.3.0/src/arena.c), arena 0 initializes before the global oversize threshold is updated; [extent.c](https://github.com/jemalloc/jemalloc/blob/5.3.0/src/extent.c) separately forces reclamation above the per-arena threshold. Raising that threshold bypasses this eager path while allowing normal timed decay.

Three repeated allocate/touch/free rounds of 1 GiB + 1 GiB + 16 MiB gave these results:

- [Ten-second dirty decay with `oversize_threshold:0`](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fmwittmann%2Fhero-allocator-preflight-v2-20260916): large frees still took about 12 ms and memory was reclaimed immediately.
- [Adding `muzzy_decay_ms:-1`](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fmwittmann%2Fhero-allocator-preflight-v3-20260916): frees became fast, but actual process RSS stayed around 2,082 MiB through 35 seconds, despite allocator-reported resident memory returning near baseline. This fails the memory-recovery gate.
- [Keeping `muzzy_decay_ms:0` and setting `arena.0.oversize_threshold` to `2**63` through `mallctl`](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fmwittmann%2Fhero-allocator-preflight-v4-20260916): frees took 0.06–0.24 ms; RSS fell from 2,082 MiB to 18 MiB by 15 seconds, versus an 18 MiB baseline. Dirty decay remained 10,000 ms.

The final CPU probe verified fast frees and RSS recovery for this allocation pattern in arena 0. A [corrected 64-GB200 treatment](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fmwittmann%2Fhero-checkpoint-decay-10000-coord-20260916-r3) has been submitted at production priority on `cw-us-east-08a`, with a 30-minute execution deadline and no queue-inclusive Iris timeout. It uses `background_thread:true,dirty_decay_ms:10000,muzzy_decay_ms:0,narenas:2,oversize_threshold:0` plus a startup write of `arena.<i>.oversize_threshold=2**63` on every initialized arena. It verifies effective settings before each measured window. The per-arena control is undocumented, so adopting this requires more care than the current one-line PR.

The treatment will be compared with the [completed immediate-purge control](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fmwittmann%2Fhero-checkpoint-decay-0-coord-20260916-r2): the same hero computation, synthetic batches, and five 512 GiB checkpoint saves, on source revision `7a9ef351a1` plus the diagnostic scripts stored in the submitted job commands. The control completed in about 22 minutes. Its five six-step save windows took 114.66, 109.43, 109.95, 101.47, and 102.19 seconds on rank 0; the three no-save windows took 97.56, 102.38, and 97.24 seconds. These totals exclude staging and final checkpoint synchronization; the diagnostic separately records full window wall time and container memory. The runs are sequential, so this comparison cannot eliminate changes in shared cluster conditions.

Training latency and repeated-save memory recovery remain unvalidated for this candidate. #9182 remains draft; production settings are unchanged. This experiment also does not test the separate Python GC and checkpoint-decision synchronization mechanism in #9205.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Deferred page purging did not reduce the cost of a save on one rack, and one rack does not reproduce the production slowdown. The allocator explanation for the production slowdown is still untested at production scale.

**Production cost.** On the current hero, `hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k`, I measured 79 hourly saves at steps 176000–188824 from W&B `throughput/iteration_time`. Excess time per save is the sum, over the following steps, of iteration time minus the median of the preceding clean steps. The median is 19.0 s over the next 11 steps, and 22.0 s over 30 steps. Baseline step time is 15.0 s. This is 2.4 s of blocking staging (`throughput/checkpoint_time`), then slow steps of +3.5, +3.6, +2.4, +1.7 and +0.9 s (median per step) for about 90 s. That window matches the ~74 s for all 704 processes to commit (https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/568). At an hourly cadence the cost is about 0.55% of training time.

**One-rack test.** [W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ckpt-arms-r2), [Iris job](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fmwittmann%2Fckpt-arms-r2-coord). The run used the hero model and data on 64 GB200 GPUs, with production allocator settings and GC every 100 steps. It used real model state. Each rank wrote the production per-rank share (8 GiB; 0.552 TB per save) because the write planner emulated 8 writing replicas. Saves ran every 4 minutes. Each save used the next setting in a fixed cycle, so all settings shared one allocation. Excess time per save, over the save step and the next 8 steps:

| Setting | Saves | Median excess |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Production settings | 2 | 8.9 s |
| Deferred purge: decay −1 during the save, then one purge on all ranks at the same step after commit | 3 | 8.5 s |
| `request_concurrency=128` | 2 | 8.3 s |
| `data_copy_concurrency=4` | 2 | 10.2 s |
| No save | 2 | −0.2 s |

About 3 s of each saving row is a measurement artifact. Before each save, a storage-budget check on rank 0 listed the run directory, and all ranks waited for it. The artifact is the same for each saving setting, so it does not change the comparison. Deferred purge reduced `madvise` purge calls from about 141k to 2.4k–3.9k per save on rank 0. Its single coordinated purge took 0.40–0.45 s. The run was stopped after 12 save slots, so the sample sizes are small, but the settings differ by about 1 s.

**Why one rack does not reproduce production.** On one rack, nearly all of the cost is in the step that contains staging. Staging is 1.75 s on the median rank, and the process faults in about 30 GiB of fresh staging memory. The tail after staging is short (+0.3 to +4.7 s over one or two steps). In production, most of the cost is in the ~90 s tail. During that tail, about 580 writing processes commit to one shared `manifest.ocdbt` in turn. With 64 writers, that phase ends within seconds. A rank frees its staging buffers when its own commit completes. My hypothesis: in production these frees and their purge stalls occur on different ranks at different times, and each stall makes the other ranks wait in collectives. One rack cannot test this hypothesis.

**Cadence.** The current run failed 4 times in about 7.3 days (mean time between failures about 44 h). With about 20 s per save, the Young/Daly optimum is about 40 minutes. The total of save cost plus expected rework after a failure is about 1.69% at 60 min, 1.59% at 40 min, 1.68% at 30 min and 2.5% at 15 min. A shorter cadence is worth it only if the cost per save goes down.

Next: production-scale evidence needs a multi-rack test, or a runtime switch for deferred purge on the hero. A structural change would make the commit window shorter: per-process OCDBT databases, or an OCDBT coordinator. The harness is on an unpublished branch, `agent/checkpoint-perf` (commits `8028b2edb6` and `c2587c669a`). It adds `TensorStoreWriteConfig.request_concurrency` and `emulated_replicas`, and `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/checkpoint_arms.py`.

issues.title: [grug] Hero training latency spikes during asynchronous checkpoint saves

issues.author: mcwitt-agent
issues.body:
Agent-driven experiment issue: the runs and this record were produced by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

## TL;DR

On one GB200 NVL72 rack, restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint at a fixed 4.19M tokens per step, 8K context trains at 297.0k tokens/s, 1.6% below 4K, and 16K at 292.5k tokens/s, 3.1% below 4K. The fraction of expert assignments dropped rises from 1.9e-4 at 4K to 8.3e-4 at 8K (4.5×) and 2.9e-3 at 16K (16×). The drops come from the receiving shard's per-chunk capacity; the ragged transport counts all of them as `sender_dropped` (see the correction comment). Each arm has three seeds; the seed-to-seed standard deviation is at most 0.03 MFU points and 4% to 7% of the drop fraction.

## Description

The hero plan in #8435 moves from 4K to 8K sequences at 50% of training (step ~195k) and to 65K at ~95%. These runs measure what the 8K switch costs in throughput and expert-capacity drops before it happens, with 16K as the next point and a 4K control from the same checkpoint.

Setup:

* Source: `main` at f38da1173de79f1eacd5f54bcfb88db6cb0a9f6e with no code changes. Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py`.
* Checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000`, the newest permanent hero checkpoint on 2026-09-30. The current hero run id records that it started from step 146k.
* Hardware and parallelism: one rack (16 nodes × 4 GB200), EP64, the hero's ragged all-to-all transport and capacity factor 1.15.
* Every arm keeps 4,194,304 tokens per step (65,536 per GPU), so the learning rate from the hero's heuristic (`MoeHeuristic` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py`, which scales with tokens per step and total tokens) is the same in all arms. `--schedule-steps 390251` is the hero's full schedule length, so the restored step sits at the hero's position in the learning-rate schedule.
* `qk_mult`, the multiplier on the query-key attention scale, follows the #8435 extension rule `1.3 × (0.1 × ln(seq / 4096) + 1)`.
* Each run trains steps 180000 to 180099 with the production watch interval (10) and coordinated GC interval (100). There is no eval and no checkpoint write.
* The trainer seed sets the data shuffle, so seeds 0, 1, and 2 train on different batches.
* Statistics cover steps 180010 to 180099 (90 steps). Each run contributes its median MFU, median tokens/s, and mean drop fraction; the tables report mean ± standard deviation across the three seeds. Starting the window at step 180030 instead moves no run's median MFU by more than 0.03 points.

| Arm | `--seq-len` | `--batch-size` | `--qk-mult` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K control | 4096 | 1024 | 1.3 |
| 8K | 8192 | 512 | 1.39 |
| 16K | 16384 | 256 | 1.48 |

Command for one run (8K, seed 0):

```bash
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930 --seed 0 \
  --num-steps 180100 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --batch-size 512 --seq-len 8192 --qk-mult 1.39 --gc-interval 100 \
  --restore-from s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000 \
  --version dev --run
```

## Results

| Arm | tokens/s | vs 4K | step time | MFU | drop fraction | vs 4K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | 301.9k ± 0.2k | | 13.89 s | 28.25 ± 0.02% | 1.86e-4 ± 0.08e-4 | 1× |
| 8K | 297.0k ± 0.2k | −1.6% | 14.12 s | 28.47 ± 0.02% | 8.29e-4 ± 0.39e-4 | 4.5× |
| 16K | 292.5k ± 0.3k | −3.1% | 14.34 s | 29.37 ± 0.03% | 2.94e-3 ± 0.20e-3 | 16× |

The logged `moe/receiver_drop_fraction` is zero in every run because the ragged transport hard-codes it to zero and counts receiver-capacity clipping as `sender_dropped`. Peak HBM was 103.1 GiB per GPU in every run. In every run, including the 4K control, the mean drop fraction over steps 180055 to 180099 was 0.75 to 1.00 times the mean over steps 180010 to 180054, so part of the measured drop fraction may be a transient after restore.

The live hero (11 racks, 4K) measured over steps 183310 to 183710 on 2026-09-30 had a median MFU of 26.47% and a mean drop fraction of 9.1e-5.

Caveats:

* MFU uses the analytic FLOP count, which charges more attention FLOPs per token at longer sequences (full causal attention on every fourth layer, a 2048-token window elsewhere). MFU therefore rises with sequence length while tokens/s falls. Compare arms by tokens/s.
* The one-rack 4K drop fraction is about 2× the 11-rack hero's. We have not tested the cause. The ratios between arms are the quantity to carry to the hero; an 8K hero drop fraction near 4e-4 is an extrapolation from that ratio, not a measurement.
* Each run covers 100 steps after the switch. Routing over thousands of steps at the new length is untested.
* The 8K and 16K arms change `qk_mult` together with sequence length.
* The diagnostic's peak learning rate comes from a one-rack token budget and is 0.69× the hero's. The diagnostic also leaves the attn_gate/router weight decay at 0 (the hero uses 0.02). Loss values are not comparable with the hero's.
* At 8K and 16K, XLA logged at compile time that rematerialization could only reduce its memory estimate to 193 GiB against a 161 GiB limit. The warning does not stop compilation. The runs trained normally with a runtime peak HBM of 103.1 GiB, the same as 4K, so the estimate overstated actual use.

## Links

* W&B runs (project `marin_moe`, group `moe-hero-ep`): 4K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s2-20260930); 8K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s2-20260930); 16K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s2-20260930)
* Hero plan: #8435. 262K context-parallel probe on the same hardware: #8754.

## Conclusion

At the planned 4K to 8K switch, expect about 1.6% fewer tokens per second and about 4.5× the 4K drop fraction, still below 0.1% of assignments on one rack. At 16K the costs are 3.1% and 16×.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: great! minimal speed difference. I am hoping the total grad norm can start arching downwards before we make the swap, but probably fine either way.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
I think swap to 16k context length will make the most sense, since its similar speed at 4k. Then when we want to do the first cooldown we can jump to 65k, another 4x gain. 4x jump per extension is on the more conservative side in literature. So I don't think we need to stick with 2x. Then another 4x to 262k at the very end of training.

On the 67B MoE we saw context extension 8k->65k at 20 percent into the run occur fine, with a grad spike in the first 10 steps but no loss spike. So it should be fine to swap when LR is still higher at 50 percent into the run.

The decision point during the swap is how we modify qk_mult. I think it is worth trying a couple options for 100 steps each w/ an eval at the end of each to empirically inform the decision. Deepseek empirically found their own optimal coef for MLA. The options are 1.3 × (0.1 × ln(4) + 1) -> 1.48, or 1.3 × (0.1 × ln(4) + 1)^2 -> 1.68, or we take the midpoint at 1.58. Then we with whichever shows the lowest paloma macro and uncheatable eval loss. 

It is a little surprising that the total grad norm hasn't started going down on the hero run at 47 percent in. Though it looks stable enough to not be concerning. - if we were to see substantial continual grad norm rise after swap during 100 step test, then we could consider holding off on context extension until LR is at lower position 60-80 percent into the run.

The main reason for doing the context length increase now instead of later would be to enable the earlier cooldown to have a longer window at higher context, which is particularly relevant because the current plan is to use that earlier cooldown for RL'ing experts for the first pass of the final model.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: When we change context length, we will have to be careful to make sure that every other schedule in the model still works correctly. The LR schedule, the weight decay schedule, the data mix schedule, the eval schedule, and the metrics around run_progress, and tokens_consumed.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Context-switch inventory, independently audited across data/resume, schedules/model settings, and eval/metrics against `main` at `3daf065582`. This revises the earlier inventory: **constant tokens per update preserves the schedules, but does not preserve the exact data stream**. The list below states implementation requirements and deployment prerequisites. The implementation is in draft PR [#9639](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9639), rebuilt as three commits after independent xhigh code review and lint review; no review findings remain. Formatting/type checks pass, 135 targeted tests pass, and 2,901 selected tests pass. Twelve selected-suite failures and one focused checkpoint timeout reproduce on the base revision. Accelerator rehearsal and live cutover have not been performed.

**Schedules and model configuration**

- Keep the production update at **46,137,344 tokens**: batch 11264 at 4096, 5632 at 8192, or 2816 at 16384. Pass the actual context into both the model and optimizer heuristic. This preserves the 390251-step schedule, MuonH/Adam learning rates, beta2, epsilon, warmup/decay/cooldown fractions, and gate/router weight-decay annealing. Changing only batch or only the model silently changes these quantities. The weight-decay schedule reads the restored Adam count; restore the full optimizer state.
- Preserve the existing zero-based `run_progress = global_step / 390251` convention. Bounded diagnostics currently use their early stop as the denominator; fix them to use the full schedule. Grafana ETA depends on the existing convention. Watch, GC, eval, and checkpoint step cadences remain valid at constant tokens/update; checkpoint wall-clock cadence still follows elapsed time.
- Make context length, QK multiplier, and receiver capacity explicit launch settings. The current QK scalar applies to both local and global layers. The discussion proposes 16K trials at approximately 1.48, 1.58, and 1.68; choosing a winner requires evaluation. Global-only scaling would be an additional model change, not an existing option. Do not hardcode unmeasured QK/capacity choices into a phase table.
- Model and optimizer arrays have no batch/context-shaped leaves. Restore uses the new static model configuration with the old parameter/optimizer arrays and counters. A real save/resume rehearsal must still exercise the new compiled shapes, expert routing, and attention kernels. Local RoPE remains at the 2048 window; longer global attention changes FLOPs and memory.

**Data order and resume**

- The loader has no checkpointed cursor: it seeks by global step and batch schedule. Use a constant new sequence batch on relaunch. A historical sequence-batch schedule mixing 4K and 16K units does not represent token history correctly. Rebuild the datasets and loader at the new context length.
- Set `BlockShuffleConfig(io_block_size=2**20 // seq_len, window_blocks=512, perm_type="feistel")` for the Harrier mixture. It matches the old default at 4K and preserves the outer permutation of 1Mi-token blocks and complete 512Mi-token windows at longer contexts. **It does not preserve within-window order.** Keep the seed, component order, immutable token store, and shuffle policy fixed.
- The previous 17B-token estimate was a simulation result, not a general repeat bound. Each of 200 cells can have an in-progress 512Mi-token window: their combined window size is about 107.4B tokens. Per-cell mixture cursor shifts and truncated dataset tails are separate effects. The earlier naive-relaunch estimates (2.85T repeated and 1.6T unique tokens missed) have not been independently reproduced; use them as motivation, not a correctness guarantee.
- **Retain the 49152-sequence mixture blocks.** Shrinking them with context length changes floor-rounded per-cell weights and the remainder assigned to the largest cell. A calculation with the checked-in weights at step 195125 gives about 108.9B tokens of aggregate absolute complete-block cursor shift at 16K if the blocks are shrunk.
- With unchanged mixture blocks, the main/cooldown stage starts are 108000/312192 at 4K and 8K, 108096/312192 at 16K, and 108288/311808 at 64K. The previous inventory estimated 2.95B tokens of aggregate per-cell cursor displacement for the 4K→16K change with unchanged mixture blocks and the 108000→108096 historical boundary; that numerical estimate has not been independently reproduced. Require explicit acceptance when a continuation shifts these boundaries. Do not assert identical per-cell token blocks in the acceptance gate.

**Metrics and evaluation**

- `throughput/total_tokens` remains exact at the same completed step when tokens/update stays fixed. A one-rack rehearsal using fewer actual tokens/update has different data offsets and cumulative tokens even if its optimizer uses the production token budget.
- Cumulative `total_gflops` currently reprices all past updates using the new context. Supply a verified cumulative-FLOP baseline at the completed handoff step; add the new phase's cost after that boundary, retaining the baseline on retries. At boundary N, use the parent total after N completed updates (normally logged at global step N−1). Per-step MFU should use the new FLOP cost; compare speed using tokens/s and elapsed iteration time.
- Pin canonical `eval_dropless/*` evaluation to **4K packing** so inherited parent rows and the `eval_regressed` alert compare the same packing. Run 16K evaluation under a distinct prefix in the trial. Fixed packing does not isolate the effect of training context when QK also changes: record QK and use matched-QK controls when attributing gains.
- Run evaluation after the first resumed update, with deduplication when the periodic/final hook hits the same step. The old first-step hook fires only at global update 1, otherwise the first new-context evaluation can wait until the next 3000-step boundary. Dropless evaluation must emit the watchdog's evaluation lifecycle events. Rehearse train → eval → next train, including dropless memory, before deployment.

**Rehearsal and acceptance**

1. CPU regression checks: compare 4K/8K/16K schedules and optimizer updates from restored counters; verify constant token totals, fixed shuffle-window coverage, documented mixture boundaries, fixed eval packing, resumed eval cadence, and cumulative FLOPs across retry. Exact optimizer/schedule equality is appropriate; exact shuffled batches and equal loss are not.
2. Restore the actual handoff checkpoint on one rack: use a 4K/QK1.3 control and 16K arms at QK1.48,1.58,1.68, each for 2–3 seeds × 200 steps. Add 4K controls at matching QK values if attributing a gain specifically to training context. Use `schedule_steps=390251`, production optimizer tokens/update, and gate/router weight decay 0.02. The original diagnostics used a smaller optimizer budget and zero gate/router decay. Smaller execution batches still change gradient statistics and data position; this is a rehearsal, not a production-equivalent gradient comparison.
3. Measure loss offset/drift, grad norm, router/drop metrics, tokens/s, iteration time, and peak memory. Include a dropless evaluation at each required packing and a save/resume. Record replacement acceptance/rollback thresholds for loss drift, gradient spikes, expert drops, throughput, and memory from these arms before authorizing deployment. The earlier measured context-dependent loss offsets mean the normal same-objective paired-loss gate cannot be applied unchanged.
4. During the production trial, verify LR, Adam LR, progress, token totals, mixture stage/weights, and FLOP continuity at matching completed steps. Compare windowed loss/gradient/drop/throughput statistics with the rehearsal bands. Score parent and child checkpoints on fixed held-out Paloma and uncheatable sets at both packings; keep short-context retention and long-context quality separate.

**Handoff record and remaining decisions**

Update the run ID, complete durable checkpoint, W&B fork point, source SHA, context/batch/QK/capacity, eval policy, FLOP baseline, mixture-shift acceptance, and rollback command together. The trigger should validate the child tracker has the same settings on retries and record them in #8506. Check checkpoint metadata, region-local storage headroom, and retention before the cutover. An old binary without requested permanent saves needs a forced temporary checkpoint copied to a durable prefix before pruning; each full hero copy was estimated at 4.29 TB in the earlier inventory. The previous live step/ETA is stale and must be refreshed at deployment.

Open deployment decisions: final QK and capacity, explicit acceptance of the 16K data shift, empirical trial thresholds, and the handoff checkpoint/time. A 64K or 262K phase also needs its own batch/mesh/attention and memory validation. The changes described here do not establish those later deployments as ready.

issues.author: mcwitt-agent
issues.body:
Get Grug MoE training running on one 8-GPU AMD Instinct node and measure a baseline. This is the first step toward AMD kernel work: the profile it produces picks the first kernel to write.

Nobody has run Levanter or Grug on AMD GPUs. The `gpu` extra in `lib/levanter/pyproject.toml` pins CUDA-only packages, and Iris schedules only NVIDIA GPUs, so run directly under Slurm. Each op in the training path has a pure JAX or XLA fallback (attention `reference`, `ragged_dot` `xla`), so no new kernels should be needed. Levanter's MFU table, [`lib/fray/src/fray/device_flops.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0c8ed89d02/lib/fray/src/fray/device_flops.py), has no AMD entries.

Train Snowball ([`levanter/models/snowball.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0c8ed89d02/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py)) with synthetic data. No trainer does this as-is: `experiments/grug/moe_pipeline` runs the Snowball shape on synthetic data but depends on NVIDIA's JaxPP, and `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep` has `--training-data synthetic` but a different expert layout.

Done when:

- The ROCm setup recipe is written down so someone else can follow it.
- A PR adds MI300X, MI325X and MI350X entries to `device_flops.py`.
- A comment here reports Snowball's step time, tokens/s, MFU and peak memory on one node, and the top ops by device time from a profile.

comments.author: asartran
comments.body:
# Setup Recipe

How to get JAX running on AMD Instinct GPUs (MI300X, MI350X) without a Marin-specific or cluster-specific step.

1. **Python 3.12 virtual environment.** System Pythons on HPC nodes are often too old for current JAX wheels. With [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/): `uv venv -p 3.12 .venv`. For a Marin checkout, `uv sync` instead; it creates the venv with the CUDA JAX, which the next step replaces.

2. **Install AMD's ROCm user-space libraries and the JAX ROCm plugin from AMD's wheel index**, matching the JAX version to the plugin. This needs no `rocm` module and no system ROCm beyond the kernel driver; about 10 GB of disk. Pick the device extras for your GPUs (`gfx942` for MI300X and MI325X, `gfx950` for MI350X and MI355X):

   ```bash
   uv pip install --index-url https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/ "rocm[libraries,device-gfx942,device-gfx950]==10.0.0"
   uv pip install --index-url https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/ "jax_rocm10_plugin==0.11.0+rocm10.0.0" "jax_rocm10_pjrt==0.11.0+rocm10.0.0"
   uv pip install "jax==0.11.0" "jaxlib==0.11.0"
   ```

   In a uv project, run things with `uv run --no-sync`; a plain `uv run` or `uv sync` re-locks to the CUDA JAX and removes the ROCm packages. Do not install Marin's `gpu` extra, which pins CUDA-only packages. If a cluster `rocm/*` module is loaded, unload it so the pip libraries are the ones found.

3. **Check the GPUs are visible:** `python -c "import jax; print(jax.devices())"` should list `RocmDevice`s, with `device_kind` reading `AMD Instinct MI300X` or `AMD Instinct MI350X`. `fray.device_flops` maps those names after #9568.

4. **Set these for every GPU job.** XLA command buffers (HIP graphs) corrupt memory on this stack, giving NaN gradients or segfaults after a few steps:

   ```bash
   export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer="
   export JAX_COMPILATION_CACHE_DIR=/some/shared/path/jax-cache   # a cold compile of the 67B model is ~12 minutes; warm is ~2
   ```

5. **For Levanter and Grug models**, use the portable code paths, because the default kernels are CUDA-only: `attention_implementation="reference"` in the model config, and `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla` in the environment (or `triton` for the Pallas kernel, single GPU only for now).

6. **Choose the compute dtype with the chip in mind.** XLA's grouped-GEMM lowering for `ragged_dot` applies to bf16 and fp16 on MI300X but only fp16 on MI350X; bf16 on MI350X falls back to a dense expansion over all experts that is 10-40× slower and uses far more memory (measurements in the baseline comment).

7. **Things that look like failures but are not.** The first cross-GPU collective takes 40-50 s per process to set up, with `rendezvous.cc ... may be stuck` warnings that resolve themselves. `rsmi_dev_gpu_metrics_info_get failed` at startup is harmless. Under an explicit mesh, a global batch of 1 fails in the next-token loss (a JAX slice-sharding bug); use at least two sequences per step on a single GPU.

8. **Do not run pytest with xdist on a GPU node.** Levanter's and Haliax's pytest configs use `-n auto`, which starts one worker per CPU core, each initialising ROCm and preallocating the GPU. This crashed nodes hard enough to take them out of the scheduler. Use `-p no:xdist` and `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false`, and prefer `srun` to `sbatch` so a crash does not requeue onto the next node.

comments.author: asartran
comments.body:
**Summary.** Snowball trains end to end on one 8× MI350X node, but at 0.27% MFU in bf16. One op is responsible: XLA on ROCm turns the MoE expert matmul into a dense matmul over all 256 experts, 256× the useful work, and that expansion also fills memory. ROCm does have a faster kernel for this op, but its coverage is uneven across data types and chips: on MI300X it works for bf16 and is 37× faster than the dense path; on MI350X it exists only for fp16 and is untuned. Switching the compute dtype to fp16 on MI350X makes the full model three times faster (0.83% MFU) and cuts peak memory by a third. On MI300X in bf16, with no workaround at all, the full model runs at 2.26 s per step and 2.20% MFU, 4.6× the MI350X bf16 throughput. After that, the biggest remaining cost is FSDP weight traffic, which expert parallelism should cut.

**Setup.** Harness from #9613, Slurm job 446882 on the AMD HPC Fund cluster, 2026-10-01, ROCm 10.0.0, JAX 0.11.0. The model is Levanter's `SnowballConfig` (`levanter/models/snowball.py`), the June Grug MoE recipe as implemented in Levanter, not the `experiments/grug` trainers; the Grug variants have not been run on AMD yet. Full 67B shape, bf16 compute with f32 params, Adam, per-layer remat, one 4096-token sequence per GPU (global batch 8), reference attention, XLA `ragged_dot`, FSDP only.

```
RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer= \
  python experiments/grug/snowball_synthetic/train.py --size full --steps 20 --profile-steps 3
```

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Step time, median of steps 2-19 | 10.3 s |
| Throughput | 3,176 tokens/s |
| MFU | 0.27% of the 2.31 PFLOP/s bf16 peak per GPU (15.9 GFLOP per token for training, counting Snowball's seven full-attention layers as in #9633) |
| Peak memory | 206 of 216 GiB per GPU |
| Compile | about 2 min with a warm compilation cache, about 12 min cold |
| Loss | 11.79 throughout; the floor for random tokens is 11.76, so nothing leaks |

**This is two orders of magnitude below the hero run, and that is the expected shape of an unoptimized first port.** MFU is computed the same way as for the hero runs: the GB200 hero sits around 26%, and the 65K-context H100 run in #9277 at 15.5%. The best AMD number here, MI300X in bf16, is about a twelfth of the hero's. For scale, a plain 16k × 16k bf16 matmul on this node runs at 1,100 TFLOP/s per GPU, 48% of the rated peak, and the model manages 6 TFLOP/s per GPU. Four things stack up: the dense expansion described below; one 4096-token sequence per GPU, so each expert GEMM sees only 64 rows; no expert parallelism, so every parameter is gathered over the network each step; and reference attention.

**Almost all the time is taken by one op, the routed-expert matmul.** From a profile of steps 10-12, per GPU per step:

| | Time | Share of step |
|---|---|---|
| Expert `ragged_dot`, forward and backward | 5.1 s | 49% |
| Expert `ragged_dot`, recomputed by remat | 1.9 s | 19% |
| RCCL collectives (FSDP) | 1.35 s | 13% |
| Transposes and masks around the expert GEMMs | 1.6 s | 15% |
| Everything else: attention, router, loss, optimizer | under 0.3 s | under 3% |

**XLA implements the routed-expert matmul on MI350X in bf16 as a dense matmul over every expert.** Each token-expert assignment is multiplied against all 256 experts' weights and the 255 unwanted results are masked away afterwards. An HLO dump of the 4-layer model shows it directly, with GEMM shapes like `[4096, 655360] × [655360, 2560]` where 655360 is 256 experts × 2560 hidden: 256× the useful FLOPs. The per-expert copies of the activations, `bf16[256, 4096, 2560]` at 5 GiB each for 4 layers and about 20 GiB each at full size, are also what fills the memory.

**A faster kernel exists, but its coverage is uneven across data types and chips.** XLA has a hipBLASLt grouped-GEMM lowering for `ragged_dot` on ROCm ([openxla/xla#38088](https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/38088)), on by default, which reads each expert's rows in place instead of copying and masking. A check in that code enables it only for bf16 and fp16 on MI300X and for fp16 on MI350X; the PR says hipBLASLt's gfx950 support was fp16-only and untuned when it landed. MI355X is the same gfx950 silicon, so the same applies there. Our bf16-on-MI350X run is the one combination on the supported chips that falls through to the dense path. Two measurements confirm it. Switching the compute dtype from bf16 to fp16 on MI350X, the same ragged dot compiles to `__cublas$lt$groupedMatmul` and runs in 3.5 ms instead of 28 ms. Running it in bf16 on MI300X instead, it also compiles to the grouped GEMM and runs in 0.75 ms, 37× faster than the dense path and 4.6× faster than the MI350X fp16 kernel, which is the untuned one.

**With fp16 compute, the full model is three times faster and uses a third less memory.** 3.4 s per step, 9,700 tokens/s, 0.83% MFU, peak memory 137 GiB instead of 206, loss still at the random-token floor. The 4-layer model gains less, 16%, because its step was never dominated by the expert matmul. The fp16 profile shows what is left: the largest item, about 1.8 s per step, is the FSDP all-gathers and reduce-scatters of the 67B parameters; the grouped GEMMs take about 1.9 s and run with 16×16 macro-tiles, the untuned MI350X path the PR warns about, with the weight-gradient GEMM (the one contracting over tokens) at 22 ms per call against 6 ms for the forward.

**What we measured.** The expert matmul rows are one GPU at the Snowball shape: 16384 token-expert rows over 256 experts, with the 2560→1280 up-projection and the 1280→2560 down-projection given as "up / down". Model rows are the harness on 8 GPUs with one sequence per GPU unless stated.

| Experiment | GPU | Compute dtype | XLA `ragged_dot` | Haliax Triton `ragged_dot` | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expert matmul, forward | MI350X | bf16 | 28.6 / 24.9 ms | 9.8 / 10.4 ms | XLA takes the dense-expansion path; Triton output matches XLA exactly |
| Expert matmul, forward + backward | MI350X | bf16 | 54.7 / 59.4 ms | 11.8 / 11.2 ms | Triton gradients match XLA, including skewed routing with 30% of experts empty |
| Expert matmul, forward | MI350X | fp16 | 3.5 / 3.1 ms | not run | XLA takes the hipBLASLt grouped-GEMM path, untuned 16×16 tiles |
| Expert matmul, forward | MI300X | bf16 | 0.75 / 0.79 ms | not run | grouped GEMM, tuned; 140 TFLOP/s of routed work |
| Expert matmul, forward | MI210 | bf16 | 239 ms | not run | dense expansion; older chip, for reference only |
| 4-layer model, 1 GPU, 2048 tokens | MI350X | bf16 | not run | 0.515 s/step | twice the per-GPU throughput of XLA's 8-GPU bf16 run |
| 4-layer model, 2 and 4 GPUs, 1024 tokens/GPU | MI350X | bf16 | not run | 1.0 s, 0.74 s/step | runs, but slower per GPU than 1 GPU; not understood |
| 4-layer model, 8 GPUs, 1024 tokens/GPU | MI350X | bf16 | 0.525 s/step, 46 GiB | segfault in step 1 | crash is right after the collectives initialise; not understood |
| 4-layer model, 8 GPUs, 1024 tokens/GPU | MI350X | fp16 | 0.44 s/step, 28 GiB | not run | |
| 4-layer model, 8 GPUs, 1024 tokens/GPU | MI300X | bf16 | 0.314 s/step, 28 GiB | not run | |
| Full 67B model, 8 GPUs, 4096 tokens/GPU | MI350X | bf16 | 10.3 s/step, 0.27% MFU, 206 GiB | not run | the baseline above |
| Full 67B model, 8 GPUs, 4096 tokens/GPU | MI350X | fp16 | 3.4 s/step, 0.83% MFU, 137 GiB | not run | |
| Full 67B model, 8 GPUs, 4096 tokens/GPU | MI300X | bf16 | 2.26 s/step, 2.20% MFU of the MI300X peak, 137 GiB | not run | 4.6× the MI350X bf16 throughput; the best configuration measured |

The setup recipe is in the [Setup Recipe comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9462#issuecomment-5942056543) on this issue.


**Problems found along the way.**
- XLA command buffers (HIP graphs) corrupt memory on this ROCm stack: NaN gradients and segfaults after a few steps. Everything here runs with them off.
- `ragged_dot` leaves rows past `sum(group_sizes)` uninitialized on ROCm, where CPU returns zeros. Grug's ring MoE path never reads those rows.
- Under an explicit mesh, JAX 0.11 drops the sharding of a `(1, 1)` slice, so the next-token loss fails at a global batch of 1. Not ROCm-specific.
- The first cross-GPU collective takes 43-48 s per process to set up.

**Next steps.** The expert matmul is still the op to fix, the same one #9077 moves to cuDNN on NVIDIA, but the cheapest win was already in XLA and gated by dtype and chip. In the order we would try them:

- Expert parallelism (`--expert-axis 8` in the harness), to stop gathering all 67B parameters every step. The fp16 profile says that traffic is now the largest cost.
- bf16 grouped GEMM on gfx950. The gate is a few lines in XLA ([openxla/xla#38088](https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/38088)); whether it can simply be relaxed depends on whether current hipBLASLt has bf16 grouped-GEMM kernels for gfx950. If it does, that is a small XLA PR; if not, the work is in hipBLASLt's kernel configurations. Both projects are open source, so this is ours to do, with AMD's input on the kernel side.
- Tuning of the grouped-GEMM tiles on gfx950, in hipBLASLt likewise. MI300X shows what tuned looks like.
- The Triton kernel as the bf16 fallback on MI350X, once its 8-GPU crash is understood.
- Whether fp16 compute is acceptable for Snowball training at all.

The full-model bf16 run on MI300X is in the table: 2.26 s per step, 14,500 tokens/s, 2.20% MFU of the MI300X peak, 137 GiB peak memory, loss at the floor. Its profile makes the first bullet concrete: of about 1.6 s of device time per step, the FSDP collectives are 1.25 s and all the expert GEMMs together about 0.25 s. On MI300X the expert matmul is no longer the problem; moving the parameters is.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
tl;dr

PivotRL (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383) is a flavor of RL that was used extensively in Nemotron-Ultra post-training. It operates on existing SFT trajectories to combine the compute efficiency of SFT with the OOD accuracy of E2E RL. PivotRL first executes local, on-policy rollouts and filters for pivots: informative intermediate turns where sampled actions exhibit high variance in outcomes; then it utilizes rewards for functional-equivalent actions rather than demanding strict string matching with the SFT data demonstration.

MarinSkyRL training data resolves to two kinds, a plain directory (`ArtifactDataSource`) and a TaskTrove parquet cohort (`TaskTroveDataSource`). Neither carries per-step annotations.

Scope: a Marin data source that resolves per-step pivot annotations with artifact identity, request plumbing for them, and a `MARIN_SKYRL` pin bump (`lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py:73`) to a MarinSkyRL revision that consumes the annotations and applies step weights in the training loop.

Open questions:

- Compute pivot scores (teacher-forced NLL under the student) as a Marin
  artifact step, or accept only precomputed annotations?
- Carry detection parameters (spike threshold, pivot weight) as named
  `SkyRLSpec` fields or leave them to `config_yaml` and `overrides`?

Done when:

- A pivot-annotated source resolves to a `ResolvedDataSource` whose
  identity covers the annotations, so the step fingerprint changes when
  annotations change.
- `SkyRLLaunchRequest` carries the annotations, and the pinned MarinSkyRL
  commit applies non-uniform step weights end to end.
- Annotation-free specs keep today's fingerprints and training behavior.
- `tests/rl/test_skyrl.py` covers the new source kind and request fields.
- We can reproduce this result from the paper E2E in MarinSkyRL -> 'On GSM8K (200 problems, 182 Kimi K2.5 competition-math traces, Gemma 4 E4B student), pivot-weighted SFT at 2.5x loss scored 80.0% vs 74.5% for uniform SFT against an 85.5% base."

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
Two released NVIDIA datasets are good candidate targets for the first Snowball PivotRL experiment:

- [`nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-SWE-Pivot-v1`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-SWE-Pivot-v1), pinned at `4947a3c8ea803413a65f9eca14a96ef521b2ddf5`. The current release has 50,308 pivot rows with `trajectory_id`, prefix position, `expected_action`, and profiling counts/pass rate (`pass_rate_total` is 8 in the inspected rows).
- [`nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-Terminal-Pivot-v1`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-Terminal-Pivot-v1), pinned at `eaef26944643644c8a3dbbf361ce6128142f5976`. It has 31,111 pivot rows with `expected_answer`, `source_trajectory_uid`, and `pivot_agent_turn_index` from GLM-5.1/Terminus-2 trajectories.

These releases correct the assumption in the issue that no training data is public. They are sufficient for a method-level reproduction, but not an exact reproduction of the paper: the SWE release is not the paper's reported 87,718-example filtered set, and the Terminal release uses a later teacher/task mixture.

Prepare separate SWE and Terminal artifacts first. Split SWE by `trajectory_id` and Terminal by `metadata.source_trajectory_uid`, not by row, so neighboring prefixes from one trajectory cannot cross train/validation. The adapter should map `responses_create_params.input` to `prompt`, preserve tools and request options, carry the expected action/answer and source identity in `extra_info`, and emit a single-turn local functional-verifier environment. SWE can reuse the existing `nemotron_ultra` action comparator after normalizing the released agent name; Terminal needs an `expected_answer` verifier case. The raw Hugging Face rows are not yet SkyRL-shaped and should not be passed directly to `PromptDataset`.

For iteration, use the two Harbor evals already implemented in Marin:

- SWE-bench Verified random-100: `swebench`
- Terminal-Bench 2.1: `tb2`

Both are in-distribution for this experiment and are safe to inspect and hill climb. Keep the policy's OOD suite untouched until the checkpoint and hyperparameters are frozen. The current launcher command is:

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model <registered-snowball-pivot-checkpoint> \
  --evals swebench,tb2 \
  --priority interactive \
  --no-wait
```

The checked-in Harbor policies use Terminus-2 + Daytona; `swebench` points at the fixed random-100 set and `tb2` points at Marin's Terminal-Bench 2 dataset. This also gives us a direct comparison with the Snowball R2E-Gym result in #9225.

Proposed training overlay below. Apply it to `cloud/iris/configs/snowball_ultra_rlvr1_split64.yaml` so the tested Megatron/vLLM placement and model geometry remain unchanged. `<...>` values are immutable prepared artifacts produced from one of the pinned releases above. Run SWE and Terminal as separate primary arms; a balanced mixture is a follow-up experiment.

```yaml
# snowball_pivotrl_split64.yaml: overlay on snowball_ultra_rlvr1_split64.yaml
entrypoint: standard

context_budget:
  request_window_tokens: 65536
  max_turns: 1
  max_new_tokens_per_turn: null  # proposed: use all context remaining after this row's prefix

trainer:
  strategy: megatron
  seed: 42
  algorithm:
    advantage_estimator: grpo
    grpo_norm_by_std: true
    advantage_batch_normalize: false
    eps_clip_low: 0.2
    eps_clip_high: 0.2
    use_entropy_loss: false
    use_kl_in_reward: false
    use_kl_loss: true
    kl_loss_coef: 0.001
    loss_reduction: token_mean
    dynamic_sampling:
      type: null                 # frozen released pivots: closest paper-like arm
      max_sample_batches: 30
      min_replace_ratio: 0.3
      informative_on: unshaped
      min_reward_std: 0.0
  epochs: 1
  max_steps: 130                # paper's disclosed SWE run length
  update_epochs_per_batch: 1
  train_batch_size: 64          # 64 unique pivot prefixes
  policy_mini_batch_size: 1024  # 64 prefixes x 16 responses
  eval_batch_size: 100
  micro_forward_batch_size_per_gpu: 1
  micro_train_batch_size_per_gpu: 1
  use_sample_packing: true
  eval_before_train: true
  eval_interval: 10
  ckpt_interval: 10
  max_ckpts_to_keep: 3
  resume_mode: none
  logger: wandb
  project_name: snowball-pivotrl
  # Keep policy/ref Megatron configs and split64 placement unchanged.

generator:
  backend: vllm
  n_samples_per_prompt: 16
  eval_n_samples_per_prompt: 1
  sampling_params:
    temperature: 1.0
    top_p: 1.0
    top_k: -1
  # Keep the tested split64 engine topology and Hermes tool parser unchanged.

data:
  kind: parquet
  train_data:
    - <s3://immutable-artifact/nemotron-{swe|terminal}-pivot/<hf-revision>/train.parquet>
  val_data:
    - <s3://immutable-artifact/nemotron-{swe|terminal}-pivot/<hf-revision>/validation.parquet>
  shuffle: true
```

The prepared rows should use `env_class: nemotron_ultra`; retain the existing `environment.skyrl_gym.nemotron_ultra` block. Each pivot rollout must terminate after one sampled action and use the local functional verifier.

`max_new_tokens_per_turn: null` is proposed syntax, not accepted by the current launcher. For a single-turn pivot there should be no separate generation budget: set each request's `max_tokens` to `request_window_tokens - tokenized_prefix_length` and let the model use the remaining context. `ContextBudget` currently requires a positive fixed output allowance and subtracts it from every row's prompt allowance; #9176 should make that field nullable for `max_turns: 1` (or add an equivalent remaining-context mode). Reusing the end-to-end RLVR config's 6,528-token cap would truncate valid pivot actions for no methodological reason.

The `64 x 16` geometry yields 1,024 rollout trajectories per trainer step. Confirm that count in the first rollout manifest before a full run. Start with a bounded startup/memory smoke, then run the static arm above. A Marin-specific follow-up can set `dynamic_sampling.type: filter` with `informative_on: unshaped` to replace stale all-pass/all-fail groups online; that is useful, but it is no longer the paper's frozen-pivot method.

The paper does not disclose the KL coefficient. Pre-register `0`, `0.001`, and `0.01` and report all three instead of selecting one retrospectively from SWE-bench/TB2.1. Keep reward shaping disabled so group informativeness is computed from the binary functional outcome.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Marin currently launches the external MarinSkyRL trainer through `skyrl_step()` and runs Harbor evaluations through a separate runner; this checkout has no `TaskSpec` or `RolloutEngine` implementation. MarinSkyRL [#712](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/712) already drafts native generation for stateless assistant-final tasks and Harbor execution for stateful tasks, but it is pinned to an older TaskCompendium spike and is waiting for the current package interfaces. The existing SkyRL [rollout-buffer contract](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/521) provides producer writes, typed receipts, trainer admission, and checkpoint snapshots, so the engine should use that handoff.

**Relevant code**
- [`skyrl.py#L270-L356`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L270-L356) — Marin's external training launcher.
- [`runner.py#L239-L282`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L239-L282) — separate Harbor evaluation loop.
- [MarinSkyRL #712](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/712) — draft TaskCompendium dispatch.
- [TaskCompendium grading in #9608](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9608/files) — submission and verifier contract.
- [TaskCompendium providers in #9522](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9522/files) — stateful tool execution contract.

# Rollout Engine proposal

A single `RolloutEngine.run(buffer)` should own task admission, policy-version selection, execution, grading, and the write to the existing `RolloutBuffer`. It consumes versioned `TaskSpec` values from a `DataGenerator`, uses the training policy for rollout identity and the inference policy for generation, and emits one typed result per task or reward group. The execution environment selects native chat only when the task can preserve generated token IDs and behavior logprobs; tasks needing tools, workspace state, multi-step context, or non-assistant submissions use Harbor, following #712. Harbor's reconstructed tokens must remain ineligible for objectives requiring exact behavior-policy evidence.

Implementation sequence:

1. Reconcile the issue's `rollout.py` and `environment.py` work with the current TaskCompendium PR stack: typed submissions and grading in [#9608](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9608), stateful providers in [#9522](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9522), and isolated provider execution in [#9607](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9607). Pin one package schema and update #712's old dependency before changing trainer dispatch.
2. Introduce the engine contract at the TaskCompendium/SkyRL boundary. Keep execution backends behind one task-to-result interface, and keep scheduling, capacity limits, policy-step tagging, and buffer commits in the engine. Reuse `RolloutWriter`/`RolloutBuffer`; do not create another durable queue.
3. Preserve grading and failure semantics across backends: invalid final submissions receive zero reward, infrastructure failures have no reward, and only completed graded records enter the buffer. Retain task ID, policy step, token evidence, tool observations, and verifier outcome in the record needed for replay and diagnosis.
4. Replace the four trainer rollout entrypaths only after the new path passes parity checks. Test native exact-token/logprob evidence, a stateful Harbor tool task, invalid versus infrastructure failures, duplicate/retry behavior, and buffer snapshot/restart. Then run a bounded mixed-task, one-step training smoke against the [existing recipe in #9527](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9527), checking completed groups, reward counts, and a committed optimizer step.

Costs and risks: the TaskCompendium interfaces and #712 are still under review, and Harbor trajectories lack exact behavior logprobs. Preserve the existing fail-fast eligibility check until that evidence changes. This session could not read the two linked Google Docs (HTTP 401), and `rollout-engine` is not a published branch in `marin-community/marin`; confirm those sources and the final module placement before implementation. No parallel engine PR is warranted while #712 owns the rollout dispatch work.

Open questions for the owner: Should the engine live in TaskCompendium or MarinSkyRL, with the other package supplying an adapter? Which of the four existing SkyRL paths must be removed in the first landing, and which need a staged migration?

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue + assess actionability
- [x] Research iris auth/login/credential code
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no open PRs/issues)
- [x] Post research + proposed design
- [ ] Await human sign-off on design before implementing (new feature → analysis, not PR)

# Research

Iris is pure-IAP for external clusters: the controller mints **no** user token ([`main.py#L127-L132`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/main.py#L127-L132)). `iris login` runs the desktop-OAuth browser flow and caches only a long-lived **IAP edge refresh token** per cluster at `~/.config/marin/credentials/<cluster>.json` ([`credential_store.py#L39-L56`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/credential_store.py#L39-L56)). Email + expiry are **not stored** — they live in the short-lived OIDC ID token that `IapRefreshTokenProvider` re-mints from the refresh token on each request ([`auth.py#L200-L235`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/auth.py#L200-L235)). Non-IAP clusters need no login (loopback/CIDR trust). No `login status`/`whoami` command exists today; `GetCurrentUser` RPC returns only `user_id`+`role` ([`service.py#L2774-L2785`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/service.py#L2774-L2785)), not email/expiry, and needs a live connection.

**Relevant code**
- [`main.py#L118-L180`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/main.py#L118-L180) — `iris login`; `_id_token` from the flow is **discarded** (L162)
- [`credential_store.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/credential_store.py) — per-cluster store; `load_credentials`, `credentials_dir()`, free-form `metadata`
- [`credentials.py#L77-L128`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/credentials.py#L77-L128) — `iap_edge_provider`, login-method resolution
- [`connect.py#L259-L265`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/connect.py#L259-L265) — `iap_config()` → is this cluster IAP-fronted
- [`cluster.py#L271-L280`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py#L271-L280) — `iris cluster list` uses `list_cluster_configs(IRIS_CLUSTER_CONFIG_DIRS)`

# Proposed Design

New command **`iris whoami [--all] [--format text|json]`** (a new top-level command; `login` is a plain `@iris.command()`, not a group, so `iris login status` would require converting it — a larger UX change I'd avoid). Default = current cluster; `--all` = every configured cluster.

Per cluster, dump:

| field | source |
|---|---|
| cluster | `CredentialRecord.cluster` / config name |
| login method | `iap` if `iap_config(config)` else `none (network trust)`; `not logged in` if IAP but no cached record |
| email | `email` claim of the IAP ID token |
| token expiry | `exp` claim of the IAP ID token |
| endpoint | `CredentialRecord.endpoint` |

Enumerate via `list_cluster_configs(IRIS_CLUSTER_CONFIG_DIRS)` × cached files under `credentials_dir()`.

**Open decision — where email/expiry come from (needs your call):**
1. **Mint-on-demand** (recommended): call `IapRefreshTokenProvider.get_token()` then `google.auth.jwt.decode(token, verify=False)` for `email`/`exp`. Accurate, works for logins done before this change, but makes a network call and shows the *re-minted* ID token's ~1h expiry (the cached refresh token has no fixed expiry — it's valid until revoked). On `IapLoginRequired`/refresh failure → show `expired — run iris login`.
2. **Store-at-login**: decode the already-returned `_id_token` at login (`main.py#L162`), stash `email` in `record.metadata`. No network, but only populated for future logins and can't show live expiry.

I lean #1 (offline-graceful), optionally also doing #2 so email shows without a network round-trip. Estimated ~70–90 lines + one behavior test (fake a `CredentialRecord`, assert the dump renders method/email/expiry; assert the not-logged-in path).

Per the agent rubric this is a **new feature**, so I'm holding here for a human to confirm the command name and the email/expiry source (#1 vs #2 vs both) before implementing. Reply with a preference and I'll open the PR.
